lessons.title: Laboratory safety, equipment and hazards
notes: A hazard is something that could cause harm; risk considers how likely harm is and how serious it could be. A risk assessment links a specific hazard to a control that reduces risk.

Goggles protect eyes from splashes. A measuring cylinder measures liquid volume more precisely than an ungraduated beaker. Read the bottom of a water meniscus at eye level. Follow the teacher’s method and report broken glass or spills.
lessons.worked: For heating water, hot glass is the hazard, burns are the possible harm, and a heatproof mat plus allowing cooling reduces the risk. “Be careful” alone is not a specific control.
lessons.question: Explain how to measure 25 cm³ of water and give a suitable control for a splash risk.
scheme: Use a measuring cylinder with a suitable scale
Read the meniscus at eye level
Wear eye protection to reduce the risk to eyes
lessons.mistake: Hazard and risk are related but do not mean the same thing.

cards.definition: Something with the potential to cause harm.
The likelihood and seriousness of harm occurring.

quiz.q: Which is a specific control for a splash hazard?
quiz.why: A control should state an action that reduces the identified risk.

misconception.q: In this lesson on laboratory safety, equipment and hazards, Sam says: “Simply write “be careful”.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Wear eye protection.
A control should state an action that reduces the identified risk.

lessons.title: Testable questions, predictions and variables
notes: A scientific question must connect to observations or measurements that could test it. The independent variable is changed, the dependent variable is measured and control variables are kept consistent.

State a prediction with a reason from scientific ideas. Define a useful range and intervals, identify measurable outcomes and control other factors that could affect them. Not every investigation is a fair test: some observe patterns or classify.
lessons.worked: To test the effect of water temperature on dissolving time, change temperature, measure time until a fixed sugar mass dissolves, and control water volume, stirring and particle size.
lessons.question: Identify the independent, dependent and two control variables when testing how light intensity affects pondweed oxygen production.
scheme: Independent: light intensity or a stated proxy such as lamp distance
Dependent: oxygen volume per unit time
Control temperature and carbon dioxide availability
lessons.mistake: A prediction should be testable, rather than an unsupported guess.

cards.definition: The factor deliberately changed.
The factor measured or observed.
A factor kept consistent to make a comparison fair.

quiz.q: When testing temperature against dissolving time, what is measured?
quiz.why: The dependent variable is the measured outcome, not the setting you change.

misconception.q: In this lesson on testable questions, predictions and variables, Sam says: “The temperature chosen.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Time taken to dissolve.
The dependent variable is the measured outcome, not the setting you change.

lessons.title: Plan fair tests, measurements and repeats
notes: A method must say what to do, what to measure, the units, the range and how to reduce risks. Resolution is the smallest detectable change. Accuracy concerns closeness to the true value; precision concerns the spread of repeated values.

Choose equipment with suitable range and resolution, check zero readings, repeat each condition and calculate a mean when appropriate. Repeatability uses the same method and setup; reproducibility compares different people or equipment.
lessons.worked: Timing ten oscillations and dividing by ten reduces the fractional effect of reaction time compared with timing just one. Repeating reduces random variation but cannot remove a miscalibrated clock.
lessons.question: Explain two ways to improve a measurement of the time for one pendulum swing.
scheme: Time several swings and divide by their number
Repeat and calculate a mean
Use the same start/finish position and small release angle
lessons.mistake: Repeated measurements do not fix a systematic offset.

cards.definition: The smallest change an instrument can detect.
Agreement when the same person repeats a method with the same equipment.

quiz.q: Why time ten swings instead of just one?
opts: It makes the clock perfectly accurate.
Reaction time has a smaller fractional effect.
quiz.why: The timing interval is longer, so the same reaction-time delay is a smaller fraction of it.

misconception.q: In this lesson on plan fair tests, measurements and repeats, Sam says: “It removes all systematic errors.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Reaction time has a smaller fractional effect.
The timing interval is longer, so the same reaction-time delay is a smaller fraction of it.

lessons.title: Bunsen burners and complete combustion
notes: A Bunsen burner mixes gas with air before combustion. With the air hole closed, the yellow safety flame is visible and generally cooler. Opening the air hole admits more oxygen and produces a hotter blue heating flame.

Identify the base, barrel, collar, air hole and gas inlet. Use the school’s supervised lighting routine, tie back hair, clear the workspace and use a heatproof mat. Never leave a heating flame unattended.
lessons.worked: A yellow flame can deposit soot because combustion is incomplete. More air supports more complete combustion; the blue flame is used for controlled heating under teacher supervision.
lessons.question: Explain why the air hole changes the flame and give one safety precaution when heating.
scheme: Air hole changes oxygen supply
More air supports more complete combustion and a blue flame
Tie back hair or use a heatproof mat or another specific valid control
lessons.mistake: A blue flame can be difficult to see and must still be treated as hot.

cards.definition: A chemical reaction with oxygen that transfers energy to the surroundings.
The visible yellow Bunsen flame used when not actively heating.

quiz.q: Opening a Bunsen air hole mainly changes what?
opts: The mass of the metal barrel.
The identity of the gas fuel.
quiz.why: Admitting more air supports more complete combustion and produces the blue heating flame.

misconception.q: In this lesson on bunsen burners and complete combustion, Sam says: “The identity of the gas fuel.” Explain the mistake.
ms: The air and oxygen supply.
Admitting more air supports more complete combustion and produces the blue heating flame.

lessons.title: Tables, graphs and conclusions
notes: A results table puts quantities and units in headings, then records measurements consistently. Continuous data can vary within a range; discrete data are counted; categories describe types.

Use a scatter graph for paired continuous quantities and a bar chart for categories. Put the independent variable on the horizontal axis. Choose a sensible scale, plot accurately and use a suitable trend line. A conclusion links the pattern to the question with numerical evidence.
lessons.worked: For temperatures 20, 30 and 40°C with times 80, 55 and 36 s, a conclusion is that higher temperature reduced dissolving time over this range; it fell by 44 s from 20 to 40°C.
lessons.question: Describe a suitable graph for temperature against dissolving time and write one feature of a strong conclusion.
scheme: Scatter graph with temperature on x and time on y
Label axes with units and use a suitable trend
Support the conclusion with paired numerical evidence
lessons.mistake: Correlation alone does not establish a causal mechanism.

cards.definition: Measurements that can take any value within a range.
Counts that take separate values.
An answer to an investigation question supported by evidence.

quiz.q: What supports a strong conclusion?
opts: A claim based on one favourite result.
A graph with no labelled axes.
A pattern backed by numerical evidence.
quiz.why: Evidence should link the observed relationship to the investigation question.

misconception.q: In this lesson on tables, graphs and conclusions, Sam says: “A claim based on one favourite result.” Explain the mistake.
ms: A pattern backed by numerical evidence.
Evidence should link the observed relationship to the investigation question.

lessons.title: Random errors, systematic errors and evaluation
notes: Random errors make repeated readings vary unpredictably. Systematic errors shift readings in a consistent direction. An anomaly is a result that does not fit the overall pattern and should be investigated.

Evaluate whether evidence supports the claim, using range, repeats, uncertainty and controls. Repeat a suspect measurement and record reasons before excluding it. Suggest a specific improvement linked to an identified limitation.
lessons.worked: A balance reading 2 g before an object is added produces an offset. Taring fixes that systematic error. Repeating without taring gives precise but inaccurate masses.
lessons.question: A thermometer always reads 2°C too high. Identify the error type and explain why averaging repeats will not correct it.
scheme: Systematic error
Every measurement has the same positive offset
Calibration/correction is needed; averaging retains the offset
lessons.mistake: Precision does not guarantee accuracy.

cards.definition: Unpredictable variation between measurements.
A consistent measurement bias in one direction.
A result that does not fit the overall pattern.

quiz.q: A balance always reads 2 g too high. What should be done?
opts: Correct the zero or calibration error.
quiz.why: Repeating measurements retains a consistent offset; calibration is needed.

misconception.q: In this lesson on random errors, systematic errors and evaluation, Sam says: “Average more readings without correction.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Correct the zero or calibration error.
Repeating measurements retains a consistent offset; calibration is needed.

lessons.title: Observing cells and magnification
notes: Cells are the basic structural units of organisms. A light microscope uses an objective and an eyepiece lens to magnify a specimen. Total magnification equals eyepiece magnification times objective magnification.

Start with the lowest-power objective and focus carefully, following the teacher’s instructions. Make clear pencil drawings with single outlines, proportional structures and ruled labels. Magnification and resolution are different: enlarging a blur does not reveal new detail.
lessons.worked: A ×10 eyepiece and ×40 objective give ×400 magnification. A 20 mm drawing of a 0.05 mm cell has magnification 20/0.05=400, with lengths first in the same units.
lessons.question: A microscope has a ×10 eyepiece and ×20 objective. Calculate total magnification and explain why units must match in image-size calculations.
scheme: Magnification is a ratio
Image and actual lengths must use the same units
lessons.mistake: Magnification has no unit of length.

cards.definition: Image size divided by actual size, using the same length units.
The ability to distinguish nearby details as separate.

quiz.q: A ×10 eyepiece and ×40 objective give what magnification?
quiz.why: Multiply the two lens magnifications: 10 × 40 = 400.

misconception.q: In this lesson on observing cells and magnification, Sam says: “×50.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Multiply the two lens magnifications: 10 × 40 = 400.

lessons.title: Plant and animal cells
notes: Animal and plant cells share a cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes. The membrane controls exchange; the nucleus contains genetic material. Many plant cells also have a cellulose wall and a permanent vacuole.

Chloroplasts absorb light for photosynthesis in photosynthetic plant cells. Not all plant cells contain chloroplasts, for example most root cells. Mitochondria are involved in aerobic respiration in both plants and animals.
lessons.worked: A leaf cell has chloroplasts because it is exposed to light. A root hair cell instead has a long extension suited to absorbing water and mineral ions. Both remain plant cells with walls.
lessons.question: Compare a typical leaf cell with an animal cell, giving one shared structure and two differences.
scheme: Shared structure with correct function, e.g. nucleus contains genetic material
Leaf cell has a cellulose cell wall; animal cell does not
Leaf cell has chloroplasts and usually a large permanent vacuole
lessons.mistake: Plants respire as well as photosynthesise.

cards.definition: A cell structure containing genetic material.
The boundary that controls exchange into and out of a cell.
A structure containing chlorophyll for photosynthesis.

quiz.q: Which statement about plant cells is accurate?
quiz.why: Photosynthetic cells need chloroplasts; most root cells do not receive light.

misconception.q: In this lesson on plant and animal cells, Sam says: “Every plant cell contains chloroplasts.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Root cells usually lack chloroplasts.
Photosynthetic cells need chloroplasts; most root cells do not receive light.

lessons.title: Specialised and unicellular organisms
notes: A specialised cell has features suited to a function. Structure–function explanations say how a feature helps, rather than simply naming it. A unicellular organism carries out its life processes within one cell.

A sperm cell has a tail for movement and many mitochondria to support it. A red blood cell has a biconcave shape and no nucleus in mature humans, leaving room for haemoglobin. A root hair increases absorption area.
lessons.worked: A unicellular organism such as an amoeba takes in food, exchanges substances and responds to its surroundings. It does not need organs, because the entire organism is one cell.
lessons.question: Explain two adaptations of a root hair cell.
scheme: Long hair-like extension
Larger surface area for absorption
Many mitochondria support active uptake of mineral ions
lessons.mistake: A unicellular organism is a living organism, not an incomplete multicellular animal.

cards.definition: A cell with features suited to a particular function.
An organism made of one cell.

quiz.q: Why does a root hair cell have a long extension?
opts: It makes the cell an animal cell.
It allows the root to make sunlight.
quiz.why: A larger surface area supports uptake of water and mineral ions.

misconception.q: In this lesson on specialised and unicellular organisms, Sam says: “It makes the cell an animal cell.” Explain the mistake.
ms: It increases absorption surface area.
A larger surface area supports uptake of water and mineral ions.

lessons.title: Diffusion and exchange at cells
notes: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration because of random motion. Individual particles continue moving in both directions, including at equilibrium.

A steeper concentration difference, larger exchange area and shorter diffusion distance increase net exchange rate. Water movement through a partially permeable membrane is called osmosis. Diffusion itself does not require cellular energy transfer.
lessons.worked: Oxygen concentration is higher outside a respiring cell than inside, so oxygen diffuses in. Carbon dioxide produced by respiration can diffuse out down its own concentration gradient.
lessons.question: Explain why oxygen moves into a respiring cell by diffusion.
scheme: Oxygen concentration is higher outside than inside
Particles move randomly
There is net movement down the concentration gradient through the membrane
lessons.mistake: At equilibrium particles do not stop moving.

cards.definition: Net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration due to random motion.
A difference in concentration between regions.

quiz.q: What happens at diffusion equilibrium?
opts: Particles move only uphill in concentration.
Particles still move in both directions.
quiz.why: Random motion continues, but there is no overall net transfer between equal concentrations.

misconception.q: In this lesson on diffusion and exchange at cells, Sam says: “All particles stop moving.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Particles still move in both directions.
Random motion continues, but there is no overall net transfer between equal concentrations.

lessons.title: Multicellular organisation and skeletons
notes: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs and organs work together in organ systems. A skeleton supports the body, protects organs, helps movement and produces blood cells within some bones.

A joint is where bones meet. Cartilage reduces friction at joint surfaces, ligaments connect bone to bone and tendons connect muscle to bone. Hinge joints mainly move in one plane; ball-and-socket joints allow movement in several directions.
lessons.worked: In an arm, muscle tissue forms part of the biceps muscle, an organ. The biceps pulls through a tendon on a forearm bone, rotating it about the elbow joint.
lessons.question: Describe the roles of cartilage, ligaments and tendons at a joint.
scheme: Cartilage cushions/reduces friction at articulating surfaces
Ligaments connect bones and stabilise the joint
Tendons attach muscle to bone
lessons.mistake: Bones do not actively contract to cause movement.

cards.definition: A group of cells working together in a function.
A structure made of different tissues working together.
A structure connecting bone to bone.

quiz.q: Which structure connects muscle to bone?
quiz.why: Tendons transmit a muscle’s pull to a bone; ligaments join bones.

misconception.q: In this lesson on multicellular organisation and skeletons, Sam says: “A ligament.” Explain the mistake.
ms: A tendon.
Tendons transmit a muscle’s pull to a bone; ligaments join bones.

lessons.title: Antagonistic muscles and movement investigations
notes: Muscles contract to pull and cannot actively push. Antagonistic pairs pull in opposite directions so that a limb can be moved both ways. A force can change movement or deform an object.

During elbow flexion the biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes; for extension their roles reverse. In a model or supervised dissection, identify bone, joint and tendon before relating visible motion to a pull.
lessons.worked: Pulling a tendon on a prepared wing bends a joint because the tendon transfers force from muscle to bone. Reversing the motion requires a pull from the opposing muscle system.
lessons.question: Explain why two antagonistic muscles are needed to bend and straighten an elbow.
scheme: Muscles pull when contracting and do not actively push
One muscle contracts to bend the elbow
The opposing muscle contracts to straighten it
lessons.mistake: Relaxing a muscle alone does not actively drive the reverse movement.

cards.definition: Two muscles that pull in opposite directions around a joint.
The active development of tension in a muscle.

quiz.q: Why are opposing muscles needed at an elbow?
opts: Bones contract to reverse the movement.
A contracting muscle pulls rather than actively pushing.
One muscle pushes when it relaxes.
quiz.why: One muscle pulls for one direction and the opposing muscle pulls for the reverse movement.

misconception.q: In this lesson on antagonistic muscles and movement investigations, Sam says: “One muscle pushes when it relaxes.” Explain the mistake.
ms: A contracting muscle pulls rather than actively pushing.
One muscle pulls for one direction and the opposing muscle pulls for the reverse movement.

lessons.title: Solids, liquids and gases
notes: The particle model explains physical properties through arrangement, movement and forces. Solid particles vibrate about fixed positions. Liquid particles stay close but move past one another. Gas particles move randomly far apart.

A solid keeps shape and volume; a liquid changes shape but has a fairly fixed volume; a gas spreads to fill its container and is readily compressed. These properties describe a simple model, not the literal colour or size of atoms.
lessons.worked: A syringe of gas compresses because particles have large gaps. A syringe of water compresses very little because particles are already close together. The particles themselves do not shrink.
lessons.question: Explain why a gas can be compressed much more than a liquid.
scheme: Gas particles have large gaps
Compression reduces the gaps
Liquid particles are close together and cannot be brought much closer
lessons.mistake: Gases contain particles; the gaps between them are not filled with more gas particles.

cards.definition: A state with particles vibrating about fixed positions.
A state with close particles that can move past one another.
A state with widely separated, freely moving particles.

quiz.q: Why is a gas easy to compress?
opts: There are large gaps between particles.
quiz.why: Compression mainly reduces the gaps between gas particles.

misconception.q: In this lesson on solids, liquids and gases, Sam says: “Its particles shrink under pressure.” Explain the mistake.
ms: There are large gaps between particles.
Compression mainly reduces the gaps between gas particles.

lessons.title: Changes of state and heating curves
notes: Melting is solid to liquid, freezing is liquid to solid, boiling or evaporation is liquid to gas, and condensation is gas to liquid. These are physical changes: the substance’s chemical identity stays the same.

Heating increases particle energy. During a state change in a pure substance at constant pressure, energy changes particle separation and interactions rather than raising temperature. Evaporation happens at a surface below boiling; boiling occurs throughout a liquid at its boiling point.
lessons.worked: Ice at 0°C can absorb energy while melting without its temperature increasing. The resulting liquid contains the same water molecules, now able to move past one another.
lessons.question: Explain the difference between evaporation and boiling.
scheme: Evaporation occurs at the surface
It can occur below the boiling point
Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling point for the pressure
lessons.mistake: Particles do not melt or expand individually when the bulk substance changes state.

cards.definition: Changing from solid to liquid.
Escape of particles from a liquid surface into the gas state.
Changing from gas to liquid.

quiz.q: How does evaporation differ from boiling?
opts: It changes water into a new element.
It must occur throughout the liquid.
It can occur at the surface below the boiling point.
quiz.why: Boiling occurs throughout a liquid at its boiling point for the stated pressure.

misconception.q: In this lesson on changes of state and heating curves, Sam says: “It changes water into a new element.” Explain the mistake.
ms: It can occur at the surface below the boiling point.
Boiling occurs throughout a liquid at its boiling point for the stated pressure.

lessons.title: Gas pressure and particle motion
notes: Gas pressure results from collisions of moving particles with container walls. Each collision exerts a force; pressure is force per unit area. Increasing temperature increases average particle kinetic energy.

For a fixed gas amount and container volume, heating generally increases pressure because collisions are more frequent and more forceful. Compressing a gas at the same temperature increases collision frequency per unit area.
lessons.worked: A sealed rigid container heats up while its gas particle number and volume stay constant. Faster-moving particles transfer more momentum at the walls, so pressure increases.
lessons.question: Explain why squeezing a sealed syringe of air increases its pressure.
scheme: Gas volume falls with particle number unchanged
Particles hit the walls more frequently per unit area
Pressure increases
lessons.mistake: A gas does not need gravity to exert pressure.

cards.definition: Force per unit area caused by particle collisions with surfaces.
A reduction in volume.

quiz.q: Heating a sealed rigid gas container usually does what?
quiz.why: Faster particles make more frequent and more forceful collisions with the fixed walls.

misconception.q: In this lesson on gas pressure and particle motion, Sam says: “Decreases particle number.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Increases pressure.
Faster particles make more frequent and more forceful collisions with the fixed walls.

lessons.title: Atoms, elements, compounds and mixtures
notes: An element contains one type of atom. A compound contains atoms of two or more elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions. A mixture contains substances together without those substances being chemically combined.

An atom is the smallest unit retaining an element’s chemical identity; it contains a nucleus and electrons. A molecule is a bonded group of atoms. Elements can have molecules, such as O₂, and not all compounds consist of discrete molecules.
lessons.worked: Iron is an element, water is a compound and air is a mixture. A physical separation can separate a suitable mixture, but breaking a compound into elements requires chemical change.
lessons.question: Compare a compound with a mixture using water and salty water as examples.
scheme: Water has chemically bonded hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed ratio
Salty water contains dissolved salt and water with variable proportions
A suitable physical method can separate salt from water
lessons.mistake: A molecule need not contain different elements: oxygen O₂ is an element.

cards.definition: A substance containing one type of atom.
A substance with different elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions.
Substances together without being chemically combined.

quiz.q: Which is a compound?
quiz.why: Water has hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

misconception.q: In this lesson on atoms, elements, compounds and mixtures, Sam says: “Air.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Pure water.
Water has hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

Salty water contains dissolved salt and water with variable proportions

quiz.q: Which is a compound?
quiz.why: Water has hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

misconception.q: In this lesson on atoms, elements, compounds and mixtures, Sam says: “Air.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Pure water.

lessons.title: Solutions and solubility
notes: A solute dissolves in a solvent to form a solution. The solute particles spread throughout the solvent rather than disappearing. Solubility is the maximum amount that dissolves in a given solvent amount at a stated temperature.

A saturated solution cannot dissolve more of that solute under the same conditions. Dissolving rate and solubility are different: stirring can speed up dissolving without increasing the final amount soluble at a fixed temperature.
lessons.worked: Crushing sugar increases exposed surface area and speeds dissolving. If a solution is already saturated at that temperature, adding more sugar leaves undissolved solid even after stirring.
lessons.question: Explain why stirring makes sugar dissolve faster but does not necessarily increase its solubility.
scheme: Stirring brings fresh solvent into contact with the solute
Dissolving rate increases
The maximum soluble amount at the same temperature is unchanged
lessons.mistake: Dissolved particles are still present even when the liquid looks clear.

cards.definition: A substance dissolved in a solvent.
A substance that dissolves a solute.
A solution containing the maximum dissolved solute at the stated conditions.

quiz.q: What does stirring usually increase?
opts: The maximum solubility at a fixed temperature.
The number of atoms in the salt.
quiz.why: Stirring brings fresh solvent into contact with solute; it need not change the final soluble amount.

misconception.q: In this lesson on solutions and solubility, Sam says: “The maximum solubility at a fixed temperature.” Explain the mistake.
ms: The rate of dissolving.
Stirring brings fresh solvent into contact with solute; it need not change the final soluble amount.

lessons.title: Filtration and crystallisation
notes: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a fluid. The residue stays on filter paper and the filtrate passes through. Crystallisation obtains a dissolved solid by concentrating a solution and allowing crystals to form.

Dissolved particles pass through ordinary filter paper with the solvent. For crystallisation gently evaporate some solvent, then cool and allow crystals to form; follow a supervised method for any heating.
lessons.worked: Sand and salt can be separated by adding water to dissolve the salt, filtering out sand, then concentrating and cooling the salt solution to obtain crystals.
lessons.question: Describe how to separate a dry mixture of sand and salt.
scheme: Add water and stir to dissolve the salt
Filter to retain sand while salt solution passes through
Concentrate the filtrate and crystallise the salt
lessons.mistake: Filtering salt solution does not remove the dissolved salt.

cards.definition: Material retained by a filter.
Fluid that passes through a filter.
Formation of solid crystals from a solution.

quiz.q: Can ordinary filter paper separate dissolved salt from water?
opts: Yes; every salt particle is trapped.
Yes; filtering turns salt into sand.
No; dissolved salt passes through with the water.
quiz.why: Filtration separates an insoluble solid, not dissolved particles, from a liquid.

misconception.q: In this lesson on filtration and crystallisation, Sam says: “Yes; every salt particle is trapped.” Explain the mistake.
ms: No; dissolved salt passes through with the water.
Filtration separates an insoluble solid, not dissolved particles, from a liquid.

lessons.title: Distillation and chromatography
notes: Distillation separates substances using differences in volatility: a liquid evaporates, then its vapour condenses and is collected. Paper chromatography separates dissolved components because they distribute differently between the moving solvent and the paper.

Draw a pencil baseline above solvent level for chromatography, place a small sample spot on it and allow solvent to rise. Different travel distances can suggest different substances, but one spot does not establish purity in all possible solvents.
lessons.worked: Distilling salt water collects water while salt remains in the flask. In chromatography an ink splitting into several spots shows it is a mixture of components that separate in that solvent.
lessons.question: Explain how distillation obtains pure water from salt water.
scheme: Water evaporates on heating
Vapour cools and condenses in the condenser
Salt is non-volatile under these conditions and remains behind
lessons.mistake: The condenser turns vapour into liquid; it does not filter dissolved salt.

cards.definition: Separation using evaporation followed by condensation.
Separation of components that move differently with a mobile phase.

quiz.q: What does a condenser do in distillation?
quiz.why: Condensation collects the evaporated solvent while non-volatile solute stays behind.

misconception.q: In this lesson on distillation and chromatography, Sam says: “Filters dissolved salt from liquid.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Cools vapour back into liquid.
Condensation collects the evaporated solvent while non-volatile solute stays behind.

lessons.title: Energy stores, transfers and dissipation
notes: Energy is measured in joules and is conserved. Stores include kinetic, thermal, chemical, gravitational and elastic. Transfers occur mechanically, electrically, by heating and by radiation.
Describe where energy starts and ends, and the transfer pathway. Dissipation spreads energy into less useful stores, often the thermal stores of surroundings. The total energy has not disappeared.
lessons.worked: A falling ball transfers energy from its gravitational store to its kinetic store. After impact, energy spreads into thermal stores and sound, so the ball’s useful mechanical energy decreases.
lessons.question: Describe the main energy changes when a battery-powered lamp lights a room.
scheme: Energy begins in the battery chemical store
Transferred electrically to the lamp
Transferred by light radiation and heating to the surroundings
lessons.mistake: Energy is transferred or stored; it is not “used up” or created by a device.

cards.definition: A way of accounting for energy held in a system.
Spreading energy into less useful stores, often in the surroundings.

quiz.q: What happens to energy described as “wasted”?
opts: It is transferred into less useful stores.
quiz.why: Total energy remains conserved even when useful energy becomes dispersed.

misconception.q: In this lesson on energy stores, transfers and dissipation, Sam says: “It is destroyed.” Explain the mistake.
ms: It is transferred into less useful stores.
Total energy remains conserved even when useful energy becomes dispersed.

lessons.title: Food energy and evaluating heating experiments
notes: Food contains chemical energy. Burning a food sample can transfer energy by heating to water, but a classroom setup captures only part of the food’s energy. Compare energy per gram when masses differ.

Control water volume, starting temperature and apparatus spacing. Measure the mass burned and temperature rise. Energy can escape to air or heat apparatus; incomplete burning also makes a food comparison less reliable.
lessons.worked: If a smaller food mass heats the same water through a greater temperature rise, it may supply more captured energy per gram. This conclusion is limited unless energy losses and burning completeness are comparable.
lessons.question: Give two limitations of comparing foods by burning them beneath a tube of water.
scheme: Energy escapes to surroundings rather than all heating the water
Incomplete combustion or unequal burning changes captured energy
Control water mass and compare energy per gram
lessons.mistake: A temperature rise alone cannot compare energy content when sample masses differ.

cards.definition: Energy associated with the chemical arrangement of substances.
Energy divided by the mass of material involved.

quiz.q: Why compare food energy per gram?
opts: A temperature rise is always the full food energy.
Every food sample has the same energy.
Food samples may have different masses.
quiz.why: A fair comparison accounts for sample mass and limitations such as heat loss.

misconception.q: In this lesson on food energy and evaluating heating experiments, Sam says: “A temperature rise is always the full food energy.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Food samples may have different masses.
A fair comparison accounts for sample mass and limitations such as heat loss.

lessons.title: Renewable and non-renewable energy resources
notes: Renewable resources are replenished on a human timescale, including sunlight, wind and flowing water. Fossil fuels and nuclear fuels are non-renewable. Each resource has benefits and limitations involving reliability, cost and environmental effects.

Separate an energy resource from an energy store. Compare the service required and the evidence: wind is variable, fossil fuel burning releases carbon dioxide, and nuclear generation produces radioactive waste but low operational carbon emissions.
lessons.worked: A town may combine variable solar generation with storage and other generation. A fair evaluation considers daily and seasonal demand rather than assuming one resource always supplies a constant output.
lessons.question: Explain one advantage and one limitation of wind power compared with fossil-fuel electricity generation.
scheme: Wind is replenished and needs no fuel burning during operation
It produces low operational greenhouse-gas emissions
Output varies with wind so supply balancing is required
lessons.mistake: Renewable does not mean impact-free or always available.

cards.definition: An energy resource replenished on a human timescale.
A resource used faster than it is naturally replenished.

quiz.q: Which resource is renewable?
quiz.why: Wind is replenished naturally, although the available output varies.

misconception.q: In this lesson on renewable and non-renewable energy resources, Sam says: “Natural gas.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Wind.
Wind is replenished naturally, although the available output varies.

lessons.title: Power, electrical energy and cost
notes: Power is the rate of energy transfer: P=E/t. A watt is one joule per second. Electricity bills commonly measure energy in kilowatt-hours; 1 kWh is the energy transferred by 1 kW for 1 hour.

For energy in kWh use power in kW times time in hours, then multiply by a stated price per kWh. Convert watts to kilowatts by dividing by 1000. Reduce use by lowering power, running time or unwanted transfers.
lessons.worked: A 1200 W heater runs for 2 hours: 1.2×2=2.4 kWh. At an assumed 25 p/kWh, cost is 60 p. This is an example tariff, not a current price quote.
lessons.question: A 500 W device runs for 3 hours. At a stated 20 p/kWh, calculate its energy use and cost.
scheme: Energy 0.5×3=1.5 kWh
lessons.mistake: kW is power; kWh is energy.

cards.definition: The rate of energy transfer.
Energy transferred by a power of one kilowatt for one hour.

quiz.q: What quantity is measured in kWh?
quiz.why: Power multiplied by time gives energy; kW alone is a power unit.

misconception.q: In this lesson on power, electrical energy and cost, Sam says: “Power.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Energy.
Power multiplied by time gives energy; kW alone is a power unit.

lessons.title: Energy stores, transfers and dissipation
notes: Energy is measured in joules and is conserved. Stores include kinetic, thermal, chemical, gravitational and elastic. Transfers occur mechanically, electrically, by heating and by radiation.
Describe where energy starts and ends, and the transfer pathway. Dissipation spreads energy into less useful stores, often the thermal stores of surroundings. The total energy has not disappeared.
lessons.worked: A falling ball transfers energy from its gravitational store to its kinetic store. After impact, energy spreads into thermal stores and sound, so the ball’s useful mechanical energy decreases.
lessons.question: Describe the main energy changes when a battery-powered lamp lights a room.
scheme: Energy begins in the battery chemical store
Transferred electrically to the lamp
Transferred by light radiation and heating to the surroundings
lessons.mistake: Energy is transferred or stored; it is not “used up” or created by a device.

cards.definition: A way of accounting for energy held in a system.
Spreading energy into less useful stores, often in the surroundings.

quiz.q: What happens to energy described as “wasted”?
opts: It is transferred into less useful stores.
quiz.why: Total energy remains conserved even when useful energy becomes dispersed.

misconception.q: In this lesson on energy stores, transfers and dissipation, Sam says: “It is destroyed.” Explain the mistake.
ms: It is transferred into less useful stores.
Total energy remains conserved even when useful energy becomes dispersed.

lessons.title: Efficiency and Sankey diagrams
notes: Efficiency is useful output energy divided by total input energy, or useful output power divided by total input power. Multiply the fraction by 100 for a percentage. A Sankey diagram uses arrow width to represent transferred energy.

Decide what output is useful for the device’s purpose. Input equals total output when all pathways are included. Improve efficiency by reducing unwanted transfers, such as friction, without claiming energy has been destroyed.
lessons.worked: A lamp transfers 100 J electrically, producing 25 J as useful visible light and 75 J into unwanted thermal pathways. Efficiency=25/100=0.25=25%.
lessons.question: A motor receives 600 J and provides 450 J of useful mechanical output. Find efficiency and unwanted energy transfer.
scheme: Efficiency 450/600=0.75
Unwanted transfer 600−450=150 J
lessons.mistake: A device cannot have efficiency above 100% when the full energy input is counted.

cards.definition: Useful output energy or power divided by total input energy or power.
A diagram whose arrow widths represent energy transfers.

quiz.q: A device gives 20 J useful output from 100 J input. What is its efficiency?

misconception.q: In this lesson on efficiency and sankey diagrams, Sam says: “80%.” Explain the mistake.

lessons.title: Species, inherited and environmental variation
notes: Members of a species share many features and can generally interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Variation consists of differences between individuals; causes include inherited genetic differences, environmental effects and their interaction.

Continuous variation has a range of measurable values, such as height. Discontinuous variation has distinct categories, such as ABO blood group. Eye colour is influenced by several genes and should not be taught as a single simple dominant/recessive trait.
lessons.worked: Arm span is usually measured on a continuous scale. A blood group falls into categories. Height can reflect genes and environment, including nutrition, rather than a single cause.
lessons.question: Compare continuous and discontinuous variation, giving one suitable example of each.
scheme: Continuous values span a range, e.g. height or arm span
Discontinuous variation has distinct categories, e.g. ABO blood group
Explain why the chosen examples fit
lessons.mistake: A feature can be influenced by both genes and environment.

cards.definition: Differences between individuals.
Variation taking values across a measurable range.
Variation in distinct categories.

quiz.q: Which is a suitable continuous variable?
quiz.why: Arm span can take a range of measured values, unlike a discrete category.

misconception.q: In this lesson on species, inherited and environmental variation, Sam says: “ABO blood group.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Arm span.
Arm span can take a range of measured values, unlike a discrete category.

lessons.title: Adaptations and changing environments
notes: An adaptation is an inherited feature that can improve survival and reproduction in a particular environment. Structural, behavioural and physiological adaptations help organisms meet challenges such as water loss, temperature or obtaining food.

Explain the link from feature to function to advantage. Individuals can respond to change, but populations evolve through inherited variation across generations. A changed environment may make a previous adaptation less useful.
lessons.worked: A cactus has a waxy surface that reduces water loss, helping it survive dry conditions. Thick fur traps insulating air in cold environments but can be disadvantageous in heat.
lessons.question: Explain how a thick fur coat benefits a mammal in a cold environment and why the benefit depends on conditions.
scheme: Fur traps air
Air reduces heat transfer from the body
In warmer conditions the same insulation can hinder cooling
lessons.mistake: Organisms do not choose inherited adaptations because they need them.

cards.definition: An inherited feature that can improve survival and reproduction in an environment.
An environmental factor affecting reproductive success.

quiz.q: Which explains an inherited adaptation?
opts: It can become more common over generations.
An organism chooses a new gene when needed.
All adaptations help in every environment.
quiz.why: The advantage depends on conditions, and inherited population changes occur across generations.

misconception.q: In this lesson on adaptations and changing environments, Sam says: “An organism chooses a new gene when needed.” Explain the mistake.
ms: It can become more common over generations.
The advantage depends on conditions, and inherited population changes occur across generations.

lessons.title: Tables, graphs and conclusions
notes: A results table puts quantities and units in headings, then records measurements consistently. Continuous data can vary within a range; discrete data are counted; categories describe types.

Use a scatter graph for paired continuous quantities and a bar chart for categories. Put the independent variable on the horizontal axis. Choose a sensible scale, plot accurately and use a suitable trend line. A conclusion links the pattern to the question with numerical evidence.
lessons.worked: For temperatures 20, 30 and 40°C with times 80, 55 and 36 s, a conclusion is that higher temperature reduced dissolving time over this range; it fell by 44 s from 20 to 40°C.
lessons.question: Describe a suitable graph for temperature against dissolving time and write one feature of a strong conclusion.
scheme: Scatter graph with temperature on x and time on y
Label axes with units and use a suitable trend
Support the conclusion with paired numerical evidence
lessons.mistake: Correlation alone does not establish a causal mechanism.

cards.definition: Measurements that can take any value within a range.
Counts that take separate values.
An answer to an investigation question supported by evidence.

quiz.q: What supports a strong conclusion?
opts: A claim based on one favourite result.
A graph with no labelled axes.
A pattern backed by numerical evidence.
quiz.why: Evidence should link the observed relationship to the investigation question.

misconception.q: In this lesson on tables, graphs and conclusions, Sam says: “A claim based on one favourite result.” Explain the mistake.
ms: A pattern backed by numerical evidence.
Evidence should link the observed relationship to the investigation question.

lessons.title: Adolescence and reproductive systems
notes: Puberty involves hormone-controlled physical changes that lead to sexual maturity; adolescence includes wider physical, emotional and social development. Timing varies between individuals. The reproductive systems produce gametes and support reproduction.

Testes produce sperm; sperm ducts carry sperm, and the penis delivers semen. Ovaries produce egg cells, oviducts carry eggs, the uterus can support pregnancy and the vagina connects to the outside. Use accurate biological vocabulary.
lessons.worked: A sperm has a flagellum for movement and genetic material in its nucleus. An egg is much larger and contains cytoplasm supporting early development. Both are gametes, carrying one set of chromosomes.
lessons.question: State the roles of the testes, ovaries and uterus.
scheme: Testes produce sperm
Ovaries produce egg cells and reproductive hormones
Uterus supports embryo/fetus development during pregnancy
lessons.mistake: Puberty does not begin at exactly the same age for everyone.

cards.definition: Hormone-controlled changes leading to sexual maturity.
A reproductive cell carrying one set of chromosomes.

quiz.q: Where are sperm produced?
quiz.why: Testes produce sperm; ovaries produce egg cells.

misconception.q: In this lesson on adolescence and reproductive systems, Sam says: “Uterus.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Testes.
Testes produce sperm; ovaries produce egg cells.

lessons.title: The menstrual cycle
notes: The menstrual cycle includes changes in the ovaries and uterine lining. Menstruation sheds the lining; the lining then rebuilds. Ovulation releases an egg from an ovary. Cycle length and ovulation timing vary.

A 28-day diagram is a teaching model, with ovulation often shown near day 14; this is not a reliable prediction for every person. If implantation occurs, hormonal signals help maintain the uterine lining.
lessons.worked: In the model cycle, the lining becomes suitable for implantation after menstruation. If no pregnancy begins, hormone changes eventually lead to its shedding and the start of another cycle.
lessons.question: Describe menstruation and ovulation, and state one limitation of a fixed 28-day cycle diagram.
scheme: Menstruation sheds the uterine lining
Ovulation releases an egg
Real cycle lengths and ovulation dates vary
lessons.mistake: Ovulation is not menstruation, and an egg is not released from the uterus.

cards.definition: Shedding of the uterine lining.
Release of an egg cell from an ovary.

quiz.q: What is a limitation of a fixed 28-day cycle diagram?
opts: Every cycle must last exactly 28 days.
Real cycle length and ovulation timing vary.
quiz.why: The diagram is a teaching model and does not predict every individual’s timing.

misconception.q: In this lesson on the menstrual cycle, Sam says: “Every cycle must last exactly 28 days.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Real cycle length and ovulation timing vary.
The diagram is a teaching model and does not predict every individual’s timing.

lessons.title: Fertilisation, implantation and fetal development
notes: Fertilisation is fusion of sperm and egg nuclei, usually in an oviduct. The resulting cell divides into an embryo. Implantation is attachment and embedding in the uterine lining, a later event.

The placenta provides an exchange surface between maternal and fetal blood supplies, which normally remain separate. Oxygen and nutrients pass to the fetus; carbon dioxide and other wastes pass back. The umbilical cord links fetus and placenta.
lessons.worked: Smoking in pregnancy can reduce oxygen supply to the fetus because carbon monoxide affects haemoglobin, and other smoke substances can cause harm. Evidence-based explanation is different from blaming an individual.
lessons.question: Distinguish fertilisation from implantation and give one role of the placenta.
scheme: Fertilisation fuses gamete nuclei, usually in the oviduct
Implantation embeds the embryo in the uterine lining
Placenta exchanges oxygen/nutrients and wastes between separate blood supplies
lessons.mistake: Maternal and fetal blood do not normally mix directly in the placenta.

cards.definition: Fusion of male and female gamete nuclei.
Embedding of an embryo in the uterine lining.
An organ allowing exchange between normally separate maternal and fetal blood supplies.

quiz.q: Where does human fertilisation usually happen?
quiz.why: Fertilisation usually precedes the embryo’s later implantation in the uterus.

misconception.q: In this lesson on fertilisation, implantation and fetal development, Sam says: “The uterine lining during implantation.” Explain the mistake.
ms: An oviduct.
Fertilisation usually precedes the embryo’s later implantation in the uterus.

lessons.title: Flower structures and pollination
notes: The stamen consists of an anther that produces pollen and a filament supporting it. The carpel includes stigma, style and ovary containing ovules. Pollination transfers pollen from anther to stigma of a compatible flower.

Insect-pollinated flowers often have petals, scent and nectar to attract insects and sticky pollen. Wind-pollinated flowers often expose anthers and feathery stigmas and make plentiful light pollen. Link each feature to pollen transfer.
lessons.worked: An insect brushes against an anther, picks up pollen and deposits some on another flower’s stigma. This transfers male gametes within pollen but is not yet fertilisation.
lessons.question: Compare one adaptation of wind-pollinated flowers with one of insect-pollinated flowers.
scheme: Wind example such as exposed feathery stigma
Explain capture of airborne pollen
Insect example such as nectar/petals attracts a carrier
lessons.mistake: Pollination is transfer of pollen; fertilisation is fusion of nuclei.

cards.definition: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma.
The part of a stamen that produces pollen.
The pollen-receiving surface of a flower.

quiz.q: Which is pollination?
quiz.why: Pollination transfers pollen; fertilisation is a later fusion of nuclei.

misconception.q: In this lesson on flower structures and pollination, Sam says: “Fusion of gamete nuclei.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Pollen reaching a compatible stigma.
Pollination transfers pollen; fertilisation is a later fusion of nuclei.

lessons.title: Plant fertilisation, seeds and dispersal
notes: After compatible pollen reaches a stigma, a pollen tube grows towards an ovule. A male nucleus fuses with an egg nucleus in fertilisation. The fertilised ovule develops into a seed, and the ovary commonly develops into a fruit.

Seed dispersal reduces competition with the parent and other seedlings. Wind, animals and explosive release move seeds in different ways. Fruit structures such as wings, hooks or fleshy tissues can support dispersal.
lessons.worked: A dandelion seed’s parachute increases air resistance and helps wind transport. A hooked fruit attaches to fur and can be carried away before falling off. Neither process is fertilisation.
lessons.question: Describe the sequence from pollination to seed formation.
scheme: Pollen arrives at a compatible stigma
A pollen tube grows to an ovule and male/egg nuclei fuse
The ovule develops into a seed
lessons.mistake: Plants form seeds after fertilisation; implantation is a term used for embryos in animal reproduction.

cards.definition: Movement of seeds away from the parent plant.
A structure in the ovary that can develop into a seed after fertilisation.

quiz.q: What commonly develops into a seed?
quiz.why: The ovule becomes the seed; the ovary commonly develops into the fruit.

misconception.q: In this lesson on plant fertilisation, seeds and dispersal, Sam says: “The whole anther.” Explain the mistake.
ms: A fertilised ovule.
The ovule becomes the seed; the ovary commonly develops into the fruit.

lessons.title: Germination and experimental controls
notes: Germination is the start of growth of a seed into a seedling. Most seeds need water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Many do not require light for germination, though the growing seedling later needs light for photosynthesis.

Water activates processes and swells tissues; oxygen supports aerobic respiration; temperature affects enzyme activity. Compare conditions while keeping seed type, age and number similar. Record the proportion germinated over a fixed time.
lessons.worked: To test the need for water, compare similar seed groups at the same temperature and oxygen availability, changing only water access. Using equal numbers allows meaningful percentage comparisons.
lessons.question: Explain why a seed needs oxygen and water to germinate.
scheme: Water activates metabolic processes and allows tissues to swell
Oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration
Respiration supplies energy for growth before sufficient photosynthesis
lessons.mistake: A seed uses stored reserves initially; it does not obtain its food from soil.

cards.definition: The start of seed growth into a seedling.
A comparison group used to help interpret an investigation.

quiz.q: Which is commonly needed for seed germination?
opts: Light for every type of seed.
Soil as the seed’s food supply.
Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.
quiz.why: Seeds initially use stored reserves; many germinate without light but need oxygen for respiration.

misconception.q: In this lesson on germination and experimental controls, Sam says: “Light for every type of seed.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.
Seeds initially use stored reserves; many germinate without light but need oxygen for respiration.

lessons.title: Chemical reactions, observations and equations
notes: A chemical reaction forms new substances as atoms rearrange. Possible observations include gas production, a precipitate, temperature change or colour change, but an observation alone may also have a physical explanation.

Word equations put reactants on the left and products on the right. Atoms are conserved; they are not created or destroyed by ordinary chemical reactions. Physical changes such as melting do not change chemical identity.
lessons.worked: Magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. Magnesium oxide has different properties from the starting metal and oxygen. Melting ice instead leaves water molecules chemically unchanged.
lessons.question: Distinguish a chemical reaction from a physical change using one example of each.
scheme: Chemical reaction forms new substances, e.g. magnesium oxide from magnesium and oxygen
Physical change retains chemical identity, e.g. melting ice
Explain the contrast using the examples
lessons.mistake: Bubbles alone do not prove a reaction: boiling also makes bubbles.

cards.definition: A substance present at the start of a chemical reaction.
A substance formed in a chemical reaction.
A change that leaves chemical identity unchanged.

quiz.q: Which observation alone does not prove a chemical reaction?
opts: Evidence that a new substance formed.
A confirmed change in chemical identity.
quiz.why: Boiling also produces bubbles without making a new chemical substance.

misconception.q: In this lesson on chemical reactions, observations and equations, Sam says: “Evidence that a new substance formed.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Bubbles appearing.
Boiling also produces bubbles without making a new chemical substance.

lessons.title: Acids, alkalis, pH and concentration
notes: Acids have pH below 7 in typical aqueous school examples; neutral water has pH 7 near room temperature; alkalis have pH above 7. An alkali is a soluble base. Indicators change colour over pH ranges.

Universal indicator estimates pH; a calibrated pH probe gives a numerical reading. Concentration describes how much solute is present per solution volume. Strength concerns how fully an acid ionises and is different from concentration.
lessons.worked: Diluting a given acidic solution usually moves its pH towards 7, though not by a simple linear amount. A concentrated weak acid and a dilute strong acid cannot be compared from those labels alone.
lessons.question: Explain the difference between a concentrated acid and a strong acid.
scheme: Concentration is amount of acid per solution volume
Strength concerns extent of ionisation in water
An acid can be strong and dilute, or weak and concentrated
lessons.mistake: Strong does not mean concentrated, and weak does not mean harmless.

cards.definition: In school aqueous examples, a substance giving a solution with pH below 7.
A base that dissolves in water.
Amount of solute per volume of solution.

quiz.q: What does “concentrated” describe?
opts: Amount of solute per solution volume.
A guarantee that an acid is strong.
quiz.why: Concentration and acid strength are different properties.

misconception.q: In this lesson on acids, alkalis, ph and concentration, Sam says: “How completely an acid ionises.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Amount of solute per solution volume.
Concentration and acid strength are different properties.

lessons.title: Neutralisation and naming salts
notes: An acid reacts with a base in neutralisation. Acid + metal oxide or alkali → salt + water. An acid reacting with a carbonate also produces carbon dioxide. Salt names depend on both reactants.

Hydrochloric acid forms chlorides, sulfuric acid sulfates and nitric acid nitrates. The metal or ammonium part supplies the first part of the name. To make a soluble salt from an insoluble base, add excess base, filter, then crystallise.
lessons.worked: Copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water. Excess copper oxide can be filtered off; water is then partly evaporated so copper sulfate crystals can form on cooling.
lessons.question: Name the salt made from magnesium oxide and hydrochloric acid, and state the other product.
scheme: Magnesium supplies the first part
Hydrochloric acid forms chloride
Magnesium chloride and water
lessons.mistake: Neutralisation need not mean mixing equal volumes: concentrations and reacting amounts matter.

cards.definition: Reaction of an acid with a base.
A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by metal or ammonium ions.

quiz.q: Which salt name follows from hydrochloric acid?
quiz.why: Hydrochloric acid forms chlorides; sulfuric acid forms sulfates.

misconception.q: In this lesson on neutralisation and naming salts, Sam says: “A sulfate.” Explain the mistake.
ms: A chloride.
Hydrochloric acid forms chlorides; sulfuric acid forms sulfates.

lessons.title: Metal properties, oxidation and reactivity
notes: Metals typically conduct electricity and heat and can be shaped; non-metals have varied properties and important exceptions, such as conducting graphite. Metal + oxygen commonly forms a metal oxide.

A reactivity series compares tendencies to react. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a suitable compound in solution. Evaluate actual observations and conditions rather than assuming every metal reacts visibly with water.
lessons.worked: Iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper. Iron is more reactive than copper, so copper is deposited. Copper cannot displace iron from iron sulfate solution.
lessons.question: Predict whether zinc displaces copper from copper sulfate and explain why, given zinc is more reactive.
scheme: Zinc displaces copper
Zinc is more reactive
Products are zinc sulfate and copper
lessons.mistake: Not every metal is magnetic and not every non-metal is an electrical insulator.

cards.definition: A reaction in which a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one in a compound.
At this level, a reaction in which a substance gains oxygen.

quiz.q: Can copper displace iron from iron sulfate, if iron is more reactive?
opts: Yes, because all metals displace each other.
quiz.why: A metal displaces another only when it is more reactive under the stated conditions.

misconception.q: In this lesson on metal properties, oxidation and reactivity, Sam says: “Yes, because all metals displace each other.” Explain the mistake.
ms: No.
A metal displaces another only when it is more reactive under the stated conditions.

lessons.title: Metals with acids and water
notes: Many reactive metals react with dilute acids to make a salt and hydrogen. With hydrochloric acid the salt is a chloride. Some very reactive metals react with cold water to form a hydroxide and hydrogen; others require steam or do not react appreciably.
Use the reactivity series and the stated conditions. A small hydrogen sample gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint in a supervised test. Keep flames away from uncontrolled gas collection.
lessons.worked: Magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen. Copper does not react appreciably with dilute hydrochloric acid because it is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.
lessons.question: State the products of magnesium with dilute sulfuric acid and describe the hydrogen test.
scheme: Magnesium sulfate
Hydrogen
A small sample gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint under supervision
lessons.mistake: Do not generalise the acid reaction to every metal.

cards.definition: An ordering of metals by their tendency to react.
A small sample gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint under supervision.

quiz.q: What forms when magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
quiz.why: Metal plus a suitable dilute acid forms a salt and hydrogen.

misconception.q: In this lesson on metals with acids and water, Sam says: “Magnesium sulfate and oxygen.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen.
Metal plus a suitable dilute acid forms a salt and hydrogen.

lessons.title: Charge, static electricity and uses
notes: Electric charge can be positive or negative. Electrons carry negative charge; rubbing suitable insulating materials can transfer electrons. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Charge is conserved in the transfer.

An object gaining electrons becomes negative; one losing them becomes positive. Charged objects can attract neutral materials through charge separation. Static charge is used in applications such as paint spraying but may also cause unwanted sparks.
lessons.worked: If a plastic rod gains electrons from a cloth, the rod becomes negatively charged and the cloth positively charged. The rubbing has transferred charge rather than created extra electrons.
lessons.question: Explain why two rods that both gained electrons repel.
scheme: Both have gained negative charge
They have the same sign of charge
Like charges repel
lessons.mistake: Protons do not usually move between objects during ordinary charging by friction.

cards.definition: A particle carrying negative electric charge.
A charge imbalance that can build up on an object.

quiz.q: An insulating rod gains electrons. What is its charge?
quiz.why: Gaining negative electrons produces an overall negative charge.

misconception.q: In this lesson on charge, static electricity and uses, Sam says: “Positive.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Negative.
Gaining negative electrons produces an overall negative charge.

lessons.title: Circuit diagrams, current and charge conservation
notes: A current is a rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes with an ammeter connected in series. A complete conducting loop and a source of potential difference are needed for a steady current in a simple circuit.

Use standard circuit symbols. In a series circuit current is the same throughout. At a junction total current entering equals total leaving, so currents in parallel branches add to the supply current.
lessons.worked: If a parallel circuit has branch currents 0.2 A and 0.3 A, the supply current is 0.5 A. Current is not used up as charge passes through a lamp.
lessons.question: Two parallel branches carry 0.4 A and 0.6 A. Find the supply current and explain the rule used.
scheme: Supply current 1.0 A
Branch currents add at a junction
Charge is conserved
lessons.mistake: Charge flows through the circuit; energy is transferred to components.

cards.definition: Rate of flow of electric charge.
An instrument measuring current, connected in series.

quiz.q: What happens to current at a junction?
opts: Each branch always has the full supply current.
Total current in equals total current out.
quiz.why: Charge is conserved, so branch currents add to the current in the shared wire.

misconception.q: In this lesson on circuit diagrams, current and charge conservation, Sam says: “Current is used up.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Total current in equals total current out.
Charge is conserved, so branch currents add to the current in the shared wire.

lessons.title: Potential difference, resistance and circuit models
notes: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge and is measured in volts. Connect a voltmeter in parallel across a component. Resistance relates potential difference and current through R=V/I.

In a series circuit potential differences across components sum to the supply. Parallel branches across the same two points have the same potential difference. A circuit model can illustrate flow and energy but must not imply that charge is consumed.
lessons.worked: Across a 6 Ω resistor with current 0.5 A, V=IR=3 V. Adding a series resistor reduces current at fixed supply voltage; adding a parallel path reduces total resistance.
lessons.question: A resistor has 12 V across it and current 2 A. Calculate its resistance and state how the voltmeter is connected.
scheme: R=V/I
Voltmeter in parallel
lessons.mistake: V=IR is a relationship; constant resistance requires suitable physical conditions.

cards.definition: Energy transferred per unit charge.
Potential difference divided by current.
An instrument connected across a component to measure potential difference.

quiz.q: How is a voltmeter connected?
opts: Across nothing, with one lead unattached.
In series instead of the connecting wire.
quiz.why: Potential difference is measured between two points across a component.

misconception.q: In this lesson on potential difference, resistance and circuit models, Sam says: “In series instead of the connecting wire.” Explain the mistake.
ms: In parallel across a component.
Potential difference is measured between two points across a component.

lessons.title: Circuit diagrams, current and charge conservation
notes: A current is a rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes with an ammeter connected in series. A complete conducting loop and a source of potential difference are needed for a steady current in a simple circuit.

Use standard circuit symbols. In a series circuit current is the same throughout. At a junction total current entering equals total leaving, so currents in parallel branches add to the supply current.
lessons.worked: If a parallel circuit has branch currents 0.2 A and 0.3 A, the supply current is 0.5 A. Current is not used up as charge passes through a lamp.
lessons.question: Two parallel branches carry 0.4 A and 0.6 A. Find the supply current and explain the rule used.
scheme: Supply current 1.0 A
Branch currents add at a junction
Charge is conserved
lessons.mistake: Charge flows through the circuit; energy is transferred to components.

cards.definition: Rate of flow of electric charge.
An instrument measuring current, connected in series.

quiz.q: What happens to current at a junction?
opts: Each branch always has the full supply current.
Total current in equals total current out.
quiz.why: Charge is conserved, so branch currents add to the current in the shared wire.

misconception.q: In this lesson on circuit diagrams, current and charge conservation, Sam says: “Current is used up.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Total current in equals total current out.
Charge is conserved, so branch currents add to the current in the shared wire.

lessons.title: Food chains, webs and interdependence
notes: A food chain shows feeding relationships and energy transfer. Arrows point from food to consumer. Producers such as plants build organic substances through photosynthesis; consumers obtain them by eating other organisms.

A food web connects chains. A population change can affect several others through food availability, predation and competition. Predictions depend on other links: real ecosystems are more complex than a single chain.
lessons.worked: Grass → rabbit → fox means energy and material pass from grass to rabbits to foxes. Fewer rabbits may reduce fox food, while grass may be eaten less, if other factors remain similar.
lessons.question: In algae → water flea → small fish, predict one possible effect of fewer water fleas on each of the other populations.
scheme: Small fish may have less food and decline
Algae may face less grazing and increase
Predictions depend on other food-web links and conditions
lessons.mistake: Food-chain arrows show transfer from food to feeder, not the direction of hunting.

cards.definition: An organism that makes organic substances, usually by photosynthesis.
An organism that obtains organic material by eating other organisms.
Connected feeding relationships in a community.

quiz.q: Which way does a food-chain arrow point?
opts: From predator to prey to show hunting.
From food to the organism eating it.
quiz.why: The arrow shows the direction of energy and material transfer.

misconception.q: In this lesson on food chains, webs and interdependence, Sam says: “Always towards the producer.” Explain the mistake.
ms: From food to the organism eating it.
The arrow shows the direction of energy and material transfer.

lessons.title: Ecosystems, competition and sampling
notes: An ecosystem includes a community of organisms interacting with its non-living environment. Competition occurs when organisms require the same limited resource, such as light, water, space or prey.

Random quadrat placement reduces selection bias when estimating plant abundance. Keep quadrat size and counting rules constant and sample enough sites. A transect investigates changes along an environmental gradient rather than random distribution.
lessons.worked: If five 1 m² quadrats contain 4,6,5,3,7 daisies, mean density is 25/5=5 daisies/m². An estimate for a comparable 100 m² area is 500 daisies, with uncertainty from sampling.
lessons.question: Explain how to estimate daisy abundance in a field using quadrats.
scheme: Place quadrats at randomly selected coordinates
Count consistently and calculate mean per unit area
Multiply by total area and state sampling limitations
lessons.mistake: Choose sites randomly, not just where plants are easy to see.

cards.definition: A community and its interactions with the non-living environment.
An interaction over a shared limited resource.
A frame marking a known sampling area.

quiz.q: Why choose quadrat positions randomly?
opts: To find only the most crowded patches.
quiz.why: Random placement avoids deliberately favouring particular parts of the habitat.

misconception.q: In this lesson on ecosystems, competition and sampling, Sam says: “To guarantee identical counts.” Explain the mistake.
ms: To reduce selection bias.
Random placement avoids deliberately favouring particular parts of the habitat.

lessons.title: Speed calculations and practical measurements
notes: Average speed is distance/time. Use metres and seconds for m/s, or consistent alternatives. A speed investigation measures a known distance and the time taken to cover it.

Repeat trials, use clear start and finish markers and minimise timing error with suitable equipment. To compare methods control the route and release conditions. Averages must be based on the quantities appropriate to the question.
lessons.worked: A trolley covers 1.8 m in 3 s, giving 0.6 m/s. A 0.2 s timing uncertainty matters less for a longer timed interval, if the motion remains comparable.
lessons.question: A trolley travels 2.4 m in 4 s. Calculate its average speed and suggest a timing improvement.
scheme: Use a longer known interval or electronic timing
Link the improvement to reduced reaction-time effect
lessons.mistake: Average speed does not necessarily equal the speed at every point.

cards.definition: Total distance divided by total time.
A new measurement under the same chosen conditions.

quiz.q: A trolley travels 6 m in 3 s. Its average speed is what?
quiz.why: Divide distance by time: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s.

misconception.q: In this lesson on speed calculations and practical measurements, Sam says: “18 m/s.” Explain the mistake.
ms: 2 m/s.
Divide distance by time: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s.

lessons.title: Distance–time graphs
notes: A distance–time graph links distance and elapsed time. For a straight segment its gradient gives speed. A horizontal segment means stationary and a steeper rising segment indicates a greater speed.

Use change in distance divided by change in time between two points on the segment. Do not use a single point’s coordinates unless the segment starts at the origin. Label both axes and units when constructing a graph.
lessons.worked: A segment from (2 s,3 m) to (8 s,15 m) has speed (15−3)/(8−2)=2 m/s. The graph is not a picture of a hill or road.
lessons.question: A straight segment runs from (5 s,10 m) to (15 s,40 m). Calculate speed.
scheme: Distance change 30 m
Time change 10 s
Speed 3 m/s
lessons.mistake: An upward line means increasing distance, not necessarily increasing speed.

cards.definition: Change in the vertical quantity divided by change in the horizontal quantity.
A graph relating distance to elapsed time.

quiz.q: What does a horizontal distance–time segment show?
quiz.why: A horizontal segment has zero gradient and shows no change in distance.

misconception.q: In this lesson on distance–time graphs, Sam says: “The speed keeps increasing.” Explain the mistake.
ms: The distance stays constant.
A horizontal segment has zero gradient and shows no change in distance.

lessons.title: Tables, graphs and conclusions
notes: A results table puts quantities and units in headings, then records measurements consistently. Continuous data can vary within a range; discrete data are counted; categories describe types.

Use a scatter graph for paired continuous quantities and a bar chart for categories. Put the independent variable on the horizontal axis. Choose a sensible scale, plot accurately and use a suitable trend line. A conclusion links the pattern to the question with numerical evidence.
lessons.worked: For temperatures 20, 30 and 40°C with times 80, 55 and 36 s, a conclusion is that higher temperature reduced dissolving time over this range; it fell by 44 s from 20 to 40°C.
lessons.question: Describe a suitable graph for temperature against dissolving time and write one feature of a strong conclusion.
scheme: Scatter graph with temperature on x and time on y
Label axes with units and use a suitable trend
Support the conclusion with paired numerical evidence
lessons.mistake: Correlation alone does not establish a causal mechanism.

cards.definition: Measurements that can take any value within a range.
Counts that take separate values.
An answer to an investigation question supported by evidence.

quiz.q: What supports a strong conclusion?
opts: A pattern backed by numerical evidence.
A claim based on one favourite result.
A graph with no labelled axes.
quiz.why: Evidence should link the observed relationship to the investigation question.

misconception.q: In this lesson on tables, graphs and conclusions, Sam says: “A claim based on one favourite result.” Explain the mistake.
ms: A pattern backed by numerical evidence.
Evidence should link the observed relationship to the investigation question.

lessons.title: Forces, resultants and motion
notes: A force is a push or pull measured in newtons. Contact forces include friction and normal contact force; gravity and magnetic forces act without direct contact. A resultant is the overall vector sum.

Balanced forces give zero resultant: an object stays at rest or continues at constant velocity. An unbalanced resultant changes velocity, which may mean changing speed, direction or both. Draw force arrows from the correct object.
lessons.worked: For a trolley pushed right with 9 N and resisted left with 4 N, resultant is 5 N right. Equal 9 N opposing forces would not imply the trolley must be stationary; it could move steadily.
lessons.question: A boat has 120 N thrust forwards and 80 N drag backwards. Find the resultant and describe the resulting change in motion.
scheme: 40 N forwards
Non-zero resultant force
The boat accelerates forwards
lessons.mistake: A moving object can have balanced forces; motion alone does not require a resultant.

cards.definition: The overall vector sum of forces on an object.
Forces with zero resultant.

quiz.q: An object has balanced forces. What can it do?
opts: Remain at rest or move at constant velocity.
quiz.why: Zero resultant means velocity does not change, not that velocity must be zero.

misconception.q: In this lesson on forces, resultants and motion, Sam says: “Only remain at rest.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Remain at rest or move at constant velocity.
Zero resultant means velocity does not change, not that velocity must be zero.

lessons.title: Gravity, mass, weight and skydiving
notes: Mass measures the amount of matter in kilograms. Weight is a gravitational force in newtons: W=mg. Gravitational field strength g is force per unit mass, about 9.8 N/kg near Earth’s surface, often rounded to 10 in examples.

During a fall weight acts down and air resistance up. At first the downward resultant increases downward speed. As drag rises, the resultant decreases; at terminal velocity forces balance and speed is constant.
lessons.worked: With g=10 N/kg, a 60 kg person weighs 600 N. Opening a parachute sharply increases drag, causing an upward resultant while the person is still moving down, so downward speed decreases.
lessons.question: Explain why a falling skydiver can reach a constant speed.
scheme: Weight acts down
Air resistance increases as speed increases
At terminal speed drag equals weight and the resultant is zero
lessons.mistake: Constant speed does not mean there are no forces.

cards.definition: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms.
The gravitational force on an object.
Constant velocity reached when forces during a fall balance.

quiz.q: At terminal velocity, how do drag and weight compare?
quiz.why: Their zero resultant means the falling object no longer accelerates.
