misconception.q: In this lesson on gravity, mass, weight and skydiving, Sam says: “Weight disappears.” Explain the mistake.
ms: They are equal and opposite.
Their zero resultant means the falling object no longer accelerates.

lessons.title: Crater investigations and evaluating results
notes: A dropped object transfers gravitational energy into impact, deformation, sound and heating. A crater investigation can test how drop height affects crater diameter while controlling object and surface properties.

Use the same ball mass and size, a level reset surface and a controlled release. Measure crater diameter in more than one direction and repeat each height. A model does not reproduce all meteorite speeds, surfaces or atmospheric effects.
lessons.worked: At larger drop heights the same ball generally reaches a greater impact speed and can create a larger crater. An uneven flour surface could change measurements independently of height.
lessons.question: Identify variables and one limitation of a classroom crater experiment.
scheme: Change drop height and measure crater diameter
Control ball and surface preparation
A classroom drop has different speeds/materials from a real impact
lessons.mistake: A trend from a model is evidence under its assumptions, not proof of every real impact outcome.

cards.definition: A simplified representation used to explore an idea.
A factor kept consistent while another is changed.

quiz.q: In a drop-height crater test, what should usually stay the same?
quiz.why: Drop height is changed and crater diameter measured; ball and surface properties should be controlled.

misconception.q: In this lesson on crater investigations and evaluating results, Sam says: “The drop height.” Explain the mistake.
ms: The ball and prepared surface.
Drop height is changed and crater diameter measured; ball and surface properties should be controlled.

lessons.title: Atoms, elements, compounds and mixtures
notes: An element contains one type of atom. A compound contains atoms of two or more elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions. A mixture contains substances together without those substances being chemically combined.

An atom is the smallest unit retaining an element’s chemical identity; it contains a nucleus and electrons. A molecule is a bonded group of atoms. Elements can have molecules, such as O₂, and not all compounds consist of discrete molecules.
lessons.worked: Iron is an element, water is a compound and air is a mixture. A physical separation can separate a suitable mixture, but breaking a compound into elements requires chemical change.
lessons.question: Compare a compound with a mixture using water and salty water as examples.
scheme: Water has chemically bonded hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed ratio
Salty water contains dissolved salt and water with variable proportions
A suitable physical method can separate salt from water
lessons.mistake: A molecule need not contain different elements: oxygen O₂ is an element.

cards.definition: A substance containing one type of atom.
A substance with different elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions.
Substances together without being chemically combined.

quiz.q: Which is a compound?
quiz.why: Water has hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

misconception.q: In this lesson on atoms, elements, compounds and mixtures, Sam says: “Air.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Pure water.
Water has hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

lessons.title: Chemical symbols, compound names and formulae
notes: Each element has a chemical symbol with an uppercase first letter and an optional lowercase second letter. A formula gives element types and atom ratios, while a mixture can have variable proportions.

Co is cobalt; CO contains carbon and oxygen. In H₂O, two hydrogen atoms are represented for each oxygen atom. Compounds often have properties very different from their elements. A subscript belongs to the preceding element or bracketed group.
lessons.worked: Sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine a toxic gas; their compound sodium chloride has very different properties. The compound is not simply a mixture retaining both starting substances’ properties.
lessons.question: Explain what CO₂ represents and how it differs from a mixture of carbon and oxygen.
scheme: Carbon and oxygen are chemically bonded
One carbon to two oxygen atoms in each molecule
A mixture is not chemically bonded in a fixed proportion
lessons.mistake: Capitalisation changes the meaning of a chemical symbol.

cards.definition: A one- or two-letter label for an element, starting with a capital letter.
A representation of the elements and atom ratios in a substance.

quiz.q: What does CO₂ represent?
opts: Two carbon atoms for each oxygen atom.
One carbon atom for every two oxygen atoms.
quiz.why: The subscript 2 applies to oxygen; Co and CO have different meanings.

misconception.q: In this lesson on chemical symbols, compound names and formulae, Sam says: “Cobalt with two electrons.” Explain the mistake.
ms: One carbon atom for every two oxygen atoms.
The subscript 2 applies to oxygen; Co and CO have different meanings.

lessons.title: Metal properties, oxidation and reactivity
notes: Metals typically conduct electricity and heat and can be shaped; non-metals have varied properties and important exceptions, such as conducting graphite. Metal + oxygen commonly forms a metal oxide.

A reactivity series compares tendencies to react. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a suitable compound in solution. Evaluate actual observations and conditions rather than assuming every metal reacts visibly with water.
lessons.worked: Iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper. Iron is more reactive than copper, so copper is deposited. Copper cannot displace iron from iron sulfate solution.
lessons.question: Predict whether zinc displaces copper from copper sulfate and explain why, given zinc is more reactive.
scheme: Zinc displaces copper
Zinc is more reactive
Products are zinc sulfate and copper
lessons.mistake: Not every metal is magnetic and not every non-metal is an electrical insulator.

cards.definition: A reaction in which a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one in a compound.
At this level, a reaction in which a substance gains oxygen.

quiz.q: Can copper displace iron from iron sulfate, if iron is more reactive?
opts: Yes, because all metals displace each other.
quiz.why: A metal displaces another only when it is more reactive under the stated conditions.

misconception.q: In this lesson on metal properties, oxidation and reactivity, Sam says: “Yes, because all metals displace each other.” Explain the mistake.
ms: No.
A metal displaces another only when it is more reactive under the stated conditions.

lessons.title: Polymers and materials
notes: Polymers contain very large molecules built from repeating smaller units. Their properties depend on structure and interactions, so different polymers can be flexible, rigid, insulating or resistant to chemicals. Natural polymers include cellulose and starch.

Choose a material by linking a property to its use and considering its whole life cycle. A polymer is not automatically biodegradable. Reuse and recycling depend on polymer type, contamination and practical collection systems.
lessons.worked: An insulating plastic casing reduces contact with conducting wires. A flexible polymer may suit a bag, while a rigid one suits a container; neither use alone proves easy recyclability.
lessons.question: Give one useful polymer property for electrical cable coating and one environmental issue to consider.
scheme: Electrical insulation
Reduces contact with conducting wire
Some polymers persist as waste and need appropriate recovery/disposal
lessons.mistake: Plastic is not one substance with one universal set of properties.

cards.definition: A substance with very large molecules made from repeating units.
Capable of being broken down by biological processes under suitable conditions.

quiz.q: Which statement about polymers is accurate?
opts: All polymers are the same plastic.
quiz.why: Structure and interactions vary, so properties and disposal options differ.

misconception.q: In this lesson on polymers and materials, Sam says: “Every polymer is readily biodegradable.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Different polymers have different properties.
Structure and interactions vary, so properties and disposal options differ.

lessons.title: The periodic table and element patterns
notes: The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number. Vertical groups contain elements with related chemical behaviour; horizontal rows are periods. Metals are mainly on the left and centre, with non-metals mostly to the right.

Use symbols and table position to identify elements and patterns. Group properties are trends with exceptions, not identical properties in every member. In the school group numbering used here, halogens are Group 7 and noble gases Group 0 (modern Groups 17 and 18).
lessons.worked: Sodium and potassium are both Group 1 metals and react with water, but potassium generally reacts more vigorously. Helium and neon are noble gases with very low reactivity under ordinary conditions.
lessons.question: Describe what a group is and why grouping elements is useful.
scheme: A vertical column in the periodic table
Members show related chemical properties
This allows informed predictions about reactions
lessons.mistake: Elements in a group have similarities, not identical properties.

cards.definition: A vertical column in the periodic table.
A horizontal row in the periodic table.

quiz.q: What is a useful feature of elements in a group?
opts: They must have identical melting points.
They are all the same element.
They often have related chemical properties.
quiz.why: A group gives patterns that support predictions, while individual properties still differ.

misconception.q: In this lesson on the periodic table and element patterns, Sam says: “They must have identical melting points.” Explain the mistake.
ms: They often have related chemical properties.
A group gives patterns that support predictions, while individual properties still differ.

lessons.title: Groups 1, 7 and 0
notes: Group 1 alkali metals are soft and react with water to produce a hydroxide and hydrogen, becoming generally more reactive down the group. Group 7 halogens are non-metals whose reactivity generally decreases down the group. Group 0 noble gases are very unreactive.

A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from a halide solution. Noble gases have stable outer electron arrangements. Only trained staff carry out hazardous alkali-metal or halogen demonstrations.
lessons.worked: Chlorine displaces bromine from bromide solution, but bromine does not displace chlorine from chloride solution. Neon is used in suitable lighting applications because it is unreactive and emits characteristic light in a discharge.
lessons.question: Given chlorine is more reactive than iodine, predict chlorine’s reaction with potassium iodide solution.
scheme: Chlorine displaces iodine
Products include potassium chloride and iodine
A more reactive halogen replaces a less reactive one
lessons.mistake: Halogen reactivity trends in the opposite direction to Group 1 reactivity.

cards.definition: A reactive non-metal in school Group 7, modern Group 17.
An element in school Group 0, modern Group 18, with very low ordinary reactivity.

quiz.q: How does Group 1 reactivity generally change down the group?
quiz.why: Alkali-metal reactivity generally increases down Group 1; halogen reactivity generally decreases.

misconception.q: In this lesson on groups 1, 7 and 0, Sam says: “It decreases like the halogens.” Explain the mistake.
ms: It increases.
Alkali-metal reactivity generally increases down Group 1; halogen reactivity generally decreases.

lessons.title: Transition metals and useful properties
notes: The central transition metals commonly have high densities and melting points, conduct heat and electricity, form coloured compounds and can act as catalysts. These are general tendencies with exceptions.

Link properties to applications and distinguish elements from their compounds. A catalyst speeds a reaction and is regenerated overall. Some transition-metal compounds are hazardous even when a familiar bulk metal has common everyday uses.
lessons.worked: Copper conducts electricity well, so it is used in wires. Iron is used in structural alloys, while iron can catalyse industrial reactions. A coloured copper compound is chemically different from copper metal.
lessons.question: Explain two uses of transition metals using their properties.
scheme: Electrical conductor such as copper used in wiring
Strength/high melting point supports an appropriate structural use
Catalytic activity supports a suitable chemical use
lessons.mistake: A transition metal and its compounds need not have the same colour or hazards.

cards.definition: A substance that speeds a reaction and is regenerated overall.
One of the central metals commonly showing properties such as coloured compounds and catalytic activity.

quiz.q: Why is copper useful in electrical wiring?
opts: Every copper compound is an identical conductor.
quiz.why: A material’s properties must be linked to the job; copper metal is a good conductor.

misconception.q: In this lesson on transition metals and useful properties, Sam says: “It is an electrical insulator.” Explain the mistake.
ms: It conducts electricity well.
A material’s properties must be linked to the job; copper metal is a good conductor.

lessons.title: Gas exchange and ventilation
notes: Air enters the trachea, then bronchi and bronchioles, reaching alveoli. Alveoli provide a large exchange area, thin walls and a rich blood supply. Oxygen diffuses into blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out.

During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens, while rib movements increase chest volume; pressure in the lungs falls and air moves in. During quiet exhalation muscles relax and elastic recoil reduces volume. Ventilation moves air; respiration is a cellular process.
lessons.worked: Thin alveolar walls shorten the diffusion distance. Blood flow and ventilation maintain concentration differences, allowing continuing gas exchange rather than reaching static equilibrium.
lessons.question: Explain how the diaphragm helps inhalation.
scheme: It contracts and flattens
Thoracic volume increases and lung pressure falls
Air moves in down a pressure difference
lessons.mistake: Lungs do not actively suck oxygen into cells; pressure differences move air.

cards.definition: Movement of air into and out of the lungs.
A small air sac providing a gas-exchange surface.
A sheet of muscle helping change chest volume.

quiz.q: What happens during normal inhalation?
opts: Oxygen is made by the lungs.
The diaphragm contracts and chest volume increases.
The diaphragm relaxes and chest volume decreases.
quiz.why: Greater chest volume lowers pressure, allowing air to enter.

misconception.q: In this lesson on gas exchange and ventilation, Sam says: “The diaphragm relaxes and chest volume decreases.” Explain the mistake.
ms: The diaphragm contracts and chest volume increases.
Greater chest volume lowers pressure, allowing air to enter.

lessons.title: Drugs, alcohol, smoking and vaping
notes: A drug changes how the body works; some are medicines used under appropriate guidance and others can cause harm or dependence. Alcohol affects nervous-system function. Tobacco smoke contains harmful substances including tar and carbon monoxide.

Nicotine is addictive. Smoke damage can impair gas exchange and cilia function. Vaping is not risk-free and is not suitable for children or non-smokers; it should not be described as harmless simply because tobacco is not burned. Evaluate evidence and avoid advertising claims.
lessons.worked: A damaged gas-exchange surface reduces effective oxygen uptake. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport, giving a mechanism linking smoke exposure to reduced exercise capacity.
lessons.question: Explain two ways cigarette smoke can reduce effective oxygen supply.
scheme: Damage to alveoli reduces effective exchange area
Carbon monoxide reduces haemoglobin oxygen carriage
Connect either mechanism to reduced oxygen reaching tissues
lessons.mistake: “Less harmful than smoking” would not mean safe or appropriate for a young non-smoker.

cards.definition: A substance that changes how the body works.
A state in which stopping a substance can be difficult and may cause withdrawal effects.

quiz.q: Which statement about nicotine vaping is accurate?
opts: It is harmless because tobacco is not burned.
It is not risk-free and is not suitable for children or non-smokers.
quiz.why: Lower harm than smoking does not mean no risk; nicotine is addictive.

misconception.q: In this lesson on drugs, alcohol, smoking and vaping, Sam says: “It is harmless because tobacco is not burned.” Explain the mistake.
ms: It is not risk-free and is not suitable for children or non-smokers.
Lower harm than smoking does not mean no risk; nicotine is addictive.

lessons.title: Nutrients, balanced diets and deficiency
notes: Carbohydrates and fats supply energy; proteins support growth and repair. Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts. Fibre supports digestive function and water is required for transport and many cellular processes. A balanced diet meets individual needs over time.

Compare evidence using portions and energy needs rather than labelling one food as always good or bad. An energy imbalance can affect body mass, and deficiency can arise when a particular nutrient is insufficient. Health is influenced by many interacting factors.
lessons.worked: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin; inadequate iron can contribute to anaemia. Vitamin C deficiency can cause scurvy. Fibre is not digested into glucose by human digestive enzymes but remains useful in the diet.
lessons.question: State the roles of protein, fibre and iron.
scheme: Protein supports growth and tissue repair
Fibre helps digestive function
Iron is required for haemoglobin
lessons.mistake: Vitamins and minerals do not provide significant dietary energy.

cards.definition: A substance needed for growth, maintenance or normal body processes.
A shortage of a required nutrient.
Dietary material that supports digestive function and is not digested by human enzymes.

quiz.q: What is a role of iron in the diet?
quiz.why: Haemoglobin needs iron and supports oxygen transport.

misconception.q: In this lesson on nutrients, balanced diets and deficiency, Sam says: “Providing most dietary energy.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Making haemoglobin.
Haemoglobin needs iron and supports oxygen transport.

lessons.title: Food tests and interpreting evidence
notes: Food tests identify particular substances rather than measuring total nutritional quality. Iodine changes from orange-brown to blue-black with starch. Benedict’s reagent forms a coloured precipitate on suitable heating with reducing sugars. Biuret reagent turns purple with protein.

The emulsion test produces a cloudy white emulsion when lipids are present. Use separate samples and controls to avoid contamination and follow supervised methods; ethanol is flammable and must be kept away from naked flames.
lessons.worked: A blue-black iodine result supports starch being present. A negative starch test does not mean the sample has no carbohydrate, because simple sugars require a different test.
lessons.question: Describe a positive starch test and explain why a negative result does not show that all carbohydrate is absent.
scheme: Add iodine solution
A blue-black change indicates starch
Other carbohydrates such as sugars may be present despite a negative starch result
lessons.mistake: A food test result identifies the tested substance, not the overall health value of a food.

cards.definition: A result indicating the tested substance was detected under those conditions.
A sugar detected by Benedict’s reagent with suitable heating.

quiz.q: What is a positive starch test?
quiz.why: Iodine is used for starch; protein and reducing sugars need different tests.

misconception.q: In this lesson on food tests and interpreting evidence, Sam says: “Benedict’s stays blue.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Iodine turns blue-black.
Iodine is used for starch; protein and reducing sugars need different tests.

lessons.title: Digestion, absorption and enzymes
notes: Digestion breaks large insoluble food molecules into smaller soluble ones. The mouth starts mechanical and chemical processing; the stomach mixes food, and much digestion and absorption occur in the small intestine. The large intestine absorbs water.

Enzymes are biological catalysts with specific substrates. Amylase digests starch into sugars, proteases digest proteins and lipases digest fats. Bile helps emulsify fats and neutralise acidic stomach contents; it is not an enzyme. Villi provide a large absorption area.
lessons.worked: A large protein cannot be absorbed directly like an amino acid. Proteases break it down, then smaller products cross the intestinal wall into circulation. Gut microorganisms also contribute to normal digestive processes.
lessons.question: Explain how enzymes and villi help supply digested nutrients to the blood.
scheme: Enzymes break large molecules into smaller soluble products
Villi increase surface area
Thin exchange surfaces and blood supply support absorption
lessons.mistake: Digestion and respiration are different processes.

cards.definition: Breaking large insoluble food molecules into smaller soluble ones.
A biological catalyst.
Transfer of digested substances across the gut wall.

quiz.q: How do villi help absorption?
opts: They stop blood reaching the intestine.
They provide a large surface area.
quiz.why: A large area, thin surface and blood supply support exchange of digested nutrients.

misconception.q: In this lesson on digestion, absorption and enzymes, Sam says: “They make food molecules larger.” Explain the mistake.
ms: They provide a large surface area.
A large area, thin surface and blood supply support exchange of digested nutrients.

lessons.title: Wave properties and sound transmission
notes: A wave transfers energy without an overall transfer of the medium. Sound is a longitudinal wave: particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer, forming compressions and rarefactions. Sound needs a medium and cannot cross a vacuum.

Amplitude relates to sound intensity and perceived loudness; frequency relates to pitch. Frequency is oscillations per second in hertz. Wavelength is distance between equivalent points. Wave speed=f×λ.
lessons.worked: Increasing a speaker’s oscillation frequency raises pitch. Increasing amplitude makes the sound more intense without necessarily changing its pitch. A sound pulse travels through air while each air particle oscillates locally.
lessons.question: Explain the difference between increasing a sound’s amplitude and increasing its frequency.
scheme: Amplitude increase increases intensity/loudness
Frequency increase raises pitch
They describe different wave properties
lessons.mistake: Air particles do not travel from the speaker all the way to the listener.

cards.definition: Maximum displacement from an undisturbed position.
Number of complete oscillations per second.
A wave with oscillations parallel to energy transfer.

quiz.q: What usually changes when a sound has a higher pitch?
opts: It begins to travel through a vacuum.
quiz.why: Pitch relates to frequency; amplitude relates to intensity and perceived loudness.

misconception.q: In this lesson on wave properties and sound transmission, Sam says: “Amplitude alone increases.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Frequency increases.
Pitch relates to frequency; amplitude relates to intensity and perceived loudness.

lessons.title: Hearing, echoes and sound speed
notes: The outer ear channels sound to the eardrum, which vibrates. The ossicles transmit vibrations to the cochlea, where receptors produce signals sent through the auditory nerve. Excessive sound exposure can damage hearing.

An echo is reflected sound. For a return trip, distance to a reflector equals speed×echo time/2. Sound travels at different speeds in different media and commonly faster in solids than gases. Loudness and speed are different properties.
lessons.worked: If an echo returns after 0.4 s and sound speed is 340 m/s, total travel distance is 136 m and the reflector is 68 m away. The division by 2 accounts for the journey there and back.
lessons.question: A sound echo returns after 0.2 s. Using 340 m/s, find the distance to the wall.
scheme: Total distance 340×0.2=68 m
Sound travels to the wall and back
Wall distance 34 m
lessons.mistake: Making a sound louder does not make it travel faster through the same air.

cards.definition: A reflected sound.
An inner-ear structure with receptors converting vibrations into nerve signals.

quiz.q: Why divide speed × echo time by two to find a wall’s distance?
opts: Sound always travels at half speed.
The sound travels to the wall and back.
quiz.why: The measured time covers a return path, twice the direct distance to the reflector.

misconception.q: In this lesson on hearing, echoes and sound speed, Sam says: “Sound always travels at half speed.” Explain the mistake.
ms: The sound travels to the wall and back.
The measured time covers a return path, twice the direct distance to the reflector.

lessons.title: Light, reflection and refraction
notes: Light is an electromagnetic wave and can travel through a vacuum. In ray diagrams straight lines show direction in a uniform medium. At a reflecting surface, angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, measured from the normal.

Refraction changes light direction when its speed changes at a boundary, except when it travels along the normal. Entering glass from air typically bends a ray towards the normal; leaving bends it away. Draw normals perpendicular to the surface.
lessons.worked: A ray incident at 35° to the normal reflects at 35° to the normal, or 55° to the surface. In glass the ray travels more slowly than in air.
lessons.question: A ray strikes a plane mirror at 40° to the normal. Give the reflection angle and its angle to the mirror surface.
scheme: Reflection angle 40° to normal
Surface is 90° to normal
Angle to surface 50°
lessons.mistake: Angles in reflection and refraction rules are measured from the normal.

cards.definition: A line perpendicular to a surface at the ray’s point of contact.
Return of a wave from a boundary.
Change in wave direction due to a change in speed across a boundary.

quiz.q: From where are reflection angles measured?
quiz.why: The normal is perpendicular to the surface and is the reference for incidence and reflection angles.

misconception.q: In this lesson on light, reflection and refraction, Sam says: “The mirror surface.” Explain the mistake.
ms: The normal.
The normal is perpendicular to the surface and is the reference for incidence and reflection angles.

lessons.title: Colour, lenses and the electromagnetic spectrum
notes: White light contains a range of visible wavelengths. A filter transmits some wavelengths and absorbs others. Objects appear coloured because of the light they reflect into the eye. A convex lens can bring parallel rays towards a focus.

The electromagnetic spectrum runs radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma in order of increasing frequency. All travel at the same speed in a vacuum; their interactions and uses differ. Lens diagrams simplify real behaviour.
lessons.worked: A red object under blue light may look dark because little blue light is reflected. A red filter does not add red light: it transmits available red wavelengths and absorbs much of the rest.
lessons.question: Explain why a red object can look dark under blue light.
scheme: It mainly reflects red wavelengths
Blue illumination contains little/no red
Much of the incident blue light is absorbed rather than reflected
lessons.mistake: A filter does not create the colour it transmits.

cards.definition: A material transmitting some wavelengths while absorbing others.
A lens that can converge parallel light rays.
A range of radiation arranged by wavelength or frequency.

quiz.q: Why may a red object look dark in blue light?
opts: It reflects little of the available blue light.
It makes its own red light.
The blue light has no energy.
quiz.why: A red object mainly reflects red wavelengths, which are missing from pure blue illumination.

misconception.q: In this lesson on colour, lenses and the electromagnetic spectrum, Sam says: “It makes its own red light.” Explain the mistake.
ms: It reflects little of the available blue light.
A red object mainly reflects red wavelengths, which are missing from pure blue illumination.

lessons.title: Chemical reactions, observations and equations
notes: A chemical reaction forms new substances as atoms rearrange. Possible observations include gas production, a precipitate, temperature change or colour change, but an observation alone may also have a physical explanation.

Word equations put reactants on the left and products on the right. Atoms are conserved; they are not created or destroyed by ordinary chemical reactions. Physical changes such as melting do not change chemical identity.
lessons.worked: Magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. Magnesium oxide has different properties from the starting metal and oxygen. Melting ice instead leaves water molecules chemically unchanged.
lessons.question: Distinguish a chemical reaction from a physical change using one example of each.
scheme: Chemical reaction forms new substances, e.g. magnesium oxide from magnesium and oxygen
Physical change retains chemical identity, e.g. melting ice
Explain the contrast using the examples
lessons.mistake: Bubbles alone do not prove a reaction: boiling also makes bubbles.

cards.definition: A substance present at the start of a chemical reaction.
A substance formed in a chemical reaction.
A change that leaves chemical identity unchanged.

quiz.q: Which observation alone does not prove a chemical reaction?
opts: Evidence that a new substance formed.
A confirmed change in chemical identity.
quiz.why: Boiling also produces bubbles without making a new chemical substance.

misconception.q: In this lesson on chemical reactions, observations and equations, Sam says: “Evidence that a new substance formed.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Bubbles appearing.
Boiling also produces bubbles without making a new chemical substance.

lessons.title: Combustion, decomposition and physical changes
notes: Combustion is reaction with oxygen that transfers energy to the surroundings. Hydrocarbon fuels undergoing complete combustion form carbon dioxide and water; incomplete combustion can form carbon monoxide or soot. Thermal decomposition breaks a compound down using heating.

Describe reactants and products with word equations. A temperature or state change need not be chemical. Conservation of atoms helps explain why a compound can change into simpler substances without matter disappearing.
lessons.worked: Calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide is a thermal decomposition. Melting wax is physical, while burning its vapour is chemical. Those processes can occur near each other in a candle.
lessons.question: Classify melting ice and heating calcium carbonate to form calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, explaining each.
scheme: Melting ice is physical
Water remains chemically water
Calcium carbonate decomposition is chemical because new substances form
lessons.mistake: Heating does not automatically mean burning.

cards.definition: Breaking down a compound by heating.
Reaction of a fuel with sufficient oxygen to form fully oxidised products.

quiz.q: Which is thermal decomposition?
opts: A compound breaking into simpler substances on heating.
A solute being filtered out of a solution.
quiz.why: Decomposition forms different substances; melting changes only physical state.

misconception.q: In this lesson on combustion, decomposition and physical changes, Sam says: “Ice melting into water.” Explain the mistake.
ms: A compound breaking into simpler substances on heating.
Decomposition forms different substances; melting changes only physical state.

lessons.title: Conservation of mass and gas exchange
notes: In an ordinary chemical reaction atoms rearrange but their total number and total mass are conserved. In a closed system total reactant mass equals total product mass. In an open container mass can enter or leave as gas.

Define the system before comparing masses. A decrease can mean gas escaped, while an increase can mean oxygen from the air joined the material. Use a suitable balance and safe closed apparatus where the method requires it.
lessons.worked: An open flask containing reacting acid and carbonate may lose mass as carbon dioxide escapes. The gas still exists outside the flask, so the total mass of all substances is conserved.
lessons.question: Explain why magnesium gains mass when burned in air.
scheme: Magnesium reacts with oxygen
Oxygen atoms become part of magnesium oxide
Including the oxygen input, total mass is conserved
lessons.mistake: Mass is not created when a solid product is heavier than the starting metal.

cards.definition: A system with no matter entering or leaving.
Total mass stays constant in an ordinary chemical reaction when all matter is counted.

quiz.q: Why can an open reaction flask lose mass?
opts: The balance converts matter into nothing.
A gas product leaves the measured flask.
quiz.why: The gas still exists outside the flask; the complete system conserves mass.

misconception.q: In this lesson on conservation of mass and gas exchange, Sam says: “Atoms are destroyed.” Explain the mistake.
ms: A gas product leaves the measured flask.
The gas still exists outside the flask; the complete system conserves mass.

lessons.title: Bonds, exothermic and endothermic reactions
notes: Breaking chemical bonds requires energy; forming bonds transfers energy out. An exothermic reaction transfers energy to surroundings overall, while an endothermic reaction transfers energy from surroundings overall.

A measured temperature rise suggests an exothermic reaction if other influences are controlled. A fall suggests endothermic behaviour. Insulation and a lid can reduce unwanted transfers; compare amounts and starting conditions fairly.
lessons.worked: A hand-warmer reaction transfers energy to its surroundings, increasing their temperature. In an endothermic cold pack, the reacting system gains energy from the surroundings, which cool.
lessons.question: Explain why an exothermic reaction can make its surroundings warmer, referring to bonds.
scheme: Energy is needed to break reactant bonds
More energy is released when product bonds form
The net transfer warms the surroundings
lessons.mistake: Bond breaking takes energy; it does not release energy by itself.

cards.definition: A process transferring energy to the surroundings overall.
A process taking energy from the surroundings overall.
A chemical link between atoms.

quiz.q: Which statement about bonds is correct?
opts: Forming bonds always requires energy overall.
quiz.why: Bond formation releases energy; the balance between breaking and forming determines the overall transfer.

misconception.q: In this lesson on bonds, exothermic and endothermic reactions, Sam says: “Breaking bonds always releases energy.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Breaking bonds requires energy.
Bond formation releases energy; the balance between breaking and forming determines the overall transfer.

lessons.title: Catalysts and enzyme activity
notes: A catalyst increases reaction rate without being used up overall. It provides a reaction pathway with lower activation energy. Enzymes are biological catalysts and depend on suitable conditions.

Compare reaction rate using the same amounts, concentration, temperature and apparatus. Collect gas volume against time or use another suitable measurable change. A catalyst changes how quickly equilibrium is reached, not the overall energy change of the reaction.
lessons.worked: For decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, a suitable catalyst gives faster oxygen production. More gas at an early time means a higher rate, not necessarily more final gas from the same limiting reactant amount.
lessons.question: Explain why faster gas production does not necessarily mean more gas will be produced in total.
scheme: Catalyst increases rate
Same reactant amount can produce the same final gas amount
The reaction reaches completion sooner
lessons.mistake: A catalyst is regenerated overall, although it participates in intermediate steps.

cards.definition: The energy barrier needed to start a reaction.
A substance that provides a faster reaction pathway and is regenerated overall.

quiz.q: What can a catalyst change for the same reactant amount?
opts: Always the final amount of gas.
Time taken to reach the final gas volume.
quiz.why: A catalyst changes rate, so completion can occur sooner without changing the final product amount.

misconception.q: In this lesson on catalysts and enzyme activity, Sam says: “The total number of atoms.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Time taken to reach the final gas volume.
A catalyst changes rate, so completion can occur sooner without changing the final product amount.

lessons.title: Aerobic respiration and exercise
notes: Aerobic respiration transfers energy from glucose in cells using oxygen. The word equation is glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Energy supports processes including muscle contraction, temperature regulation and growth.

Respiration takes place continually in plant and animal cells. During exercise muscle energy demand rises, so breathing and heart rate generally increase to support gas exchange and transport. Breathing is movement of air, not the chemical reaction of respiration.
lessons.worked: A runner’s muscles require greater rates of energy transfer. Increased ventilation brings more oxygen to alveoli and increased blood flow delivers it to tissues while carrying carbon dioxide away.
lessons.question: Explain why breathing rate usually increases during exercise.
scheme: Muscles require faster energy transfer
Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and produces carbon dioxide
Increased ventilation supports oxygen supply and carbon dioxide removal
lessons.mistake: Respiration is not the same as breathing.

cards.definition: Cellular breakdown of glucose using oxygen to transfer energy.
A set of cellular chemical processes transferring energy from organic substances.

quiz.q: Which organisms respire?
quiz.why: Plant and animal cells need energy transfer continually; photosynthesis does not replace respiration.

misconception.q: In this lesson on aerobic respiration and exercise, Sam says: “Only animals.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Plants and animals.
Plant and animal cells need energy transfer continually; photosynthesis does not replace respiration.

lessons.title: Anaerobic respiration, fermentation and biotechnology
notes: When oxygen supply cannot meet demand, human muscles can transfer energy anaerobically from glucose, producing lactate. Yeast anaerobic respiration forms ethanol and carbon dioxide; this is fermentation. Anaerobic pathways transfer less energy per glucose than aerobic respiration.

Yeast fermentation is used in bread making and producing alcoholic drinks. Investigations can compare gas production per minute while controlling yeast quantity, glucose concentration, temperature and time. Biological activity has an optimum range and can decline at high temperatures.
lessons.worked: Carbon dioxide from yeast makes dough rise; baking changes the structure and kills the yeast. Raising temperature speeds enzyme activity only up to a suitable range, not indefinitely.
lessons.question: State the products of yeast anaerobic respiration and explain how one helps bread making.
scheme: Ethanol
Carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide gas makes dough rise
lessons.mistake: Human muscle anaerobic respiration and yeast fermentation do not have identical products.

cards.definition: Energy transfer from glucose without using oxygen.
Anaerobic respiration in yeast producing ethanol and carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: Which gas helps bread dough rise?
quiz.why: Yeast fermentation produces carbon dioxide, whose bubbles expand the dough.

misconception.q: In this lesson on anaerobic respiration, fermentation and biotechnology, Sam says: “Oxygen made by yeast fermentation.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Carbon dioxide from yeast.
Yeast fermentation produces carbon dioxide, whose bubbles expand the dough.

lessons.title: Plan fair tests, measurements and repeats
notes: A method must say what to do, what to measure, the units, the range and how to reduce risks. Resolution is the smallest detectable change. Accuracy concerns closeness to the true value; precision concerns the spread of repeated values.

Choose equipment with suitable range and resolution, check zero readings, repeat each condition and calculate a mean when appropriate. Repeatability uses the same method and setup; reproducibility compares different people or equipment.
lessons.worked: Timing ten oscillations and dividing by ten reduces the fractional effect of reaction time compared with timing just one. Repeating reduces random variation but cannot remove a miscalibrated clock.
lessons.question: Explain two ways to improve a measurement of the time for one pendulum swing.
scheme: Time several swings and divide by their number
Repeat and calculate a mean
Use the same start/finish position and small release angle
lessons.mistake: Repeated measurements do not fix a systematic offset.

cards.definition: The smallest change an instrument can detect.
Agreement when the same person repeats a method with the same equipment.

quiz.q: Why time ten swings instead of just one?
opts: It makes the clock perfectly accurate.
Reaction time has a smaller fractional effect.
quiz.why: The timing interval is longer, so the same reaction-time delay is a smaller fraction of it.

misconception.q: In this lesson on plan fair tests, measurements and repeats, Sam says: “It removes all systematic errors.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Reaction time has a smaller fractional effect.
The timing interval is longer, so the same reaction-time delay is a smaller fraction of it.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and uses of glucose
notes: Photosynthesis transfers light energy into chemical stores in glucose. Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. Chlorophyll absorbs light in chloroplasts. Plants also respire at all times, including in daylight.

Glucose can be used in respiration, converted to starch for storage, used to make cellulose or combined with mineral nutrients to build other molecules. Much of a plant’s dry mass comes from carbon dioxide incorporated from the air.
lessons.worked: A green leaf in light can make glucose and release oxygen. At night photosynthesis stops without light, but respiration continues, using oxygen and producing carbon dioxide.
lessons.question: State the photosynthesis word equation and two possible uses of the glucose made.
scheme: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with light
Respiration or starch storage
Cellulose production or making other suitable compounds
lessons.mistake: Plants do not take their food from soil; they make organic substances using photosynthesis.

cards.definition: Using light to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.
A pigment that absorbs light for photosynthesis.

quiz.q: Where does much of a plant’s dry carbon come from?
opts: Mineral ions as a source of carbon.
quiz.why: Photosynthesis incorporates carbon from carbon dioxide into organic material.

misconception.q: In this lesson on photosynthesis and uses of glucose, Sam says: “Mineral ions as a source of carbon.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Carbon dioxide in the air.
Photosynthesis incorporates carbon from carbon dioxide into organic material.

lessons.title: Leaf structure, minerals and limiting factors
notes: A leaf’s broad surface intercepts light. Thin tissues shorten diffusion distances; palisade cells often contain many chloroplasts. Stomata allow gas exchange, and vascular tissues transport water and sugars.

Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature can limit photosynthesis. Nitrate ions are needed for amino acids and proteins; magnesium is needed for chlorophyll. Increasing one factor helps only if it is limiting.
lessons.worked: Adding more light may initially increase oxygen production. If carbon dioxide becomes limiting, further light produces little increase. A magnesium deficiency can reduce chlorophyll and cause yellowing.
lessons.question: Explain why increasing light intensity may eventually stop increasing photosynthesis rate.
scheme: Light initially limits rate
Another factor such as carbon dioxide becomes limiting
Increasing light alone cannot remove that new limit
lessons.mistake: Mineral nutrients are not a plant’s energy source.

cards.definition: A pore in a leaf surface that allows gas exchange.
A factor preventing the rate from increasing under the current conditions.

quiz.q: Why can extra light eventually stop increasing photosynthesis?
quiz.why: If carbon dioxide or temperature limits the rate, more light alone does not remove the limit.

misconception.q: In this lesson on leaf structure, minerals and limiting factors, Sam says: “Plants stop needing carbon dioxide.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Another factor becomes limiting.
If carbon dioxide or temperature limits the rate, more light alone does not remove the limit.

lessons.title: Pondweed, starch tests and evaluating photosynthesis evidence
notes: Oxygen production from pondweed can indicate photosynthesis rate, but net gas output also reflects respiration. Gas volume is often more reliable than bubble count because bubbles vary in size. A starch test indicates stored carbohydrate.

Control temperature and carbon dioxide while changing light. Allow time to acclimatise. In a supervised starch test, soften the leaf, decolourise it with ethanol in a hot-water bath away from flames, rinse and add iodine. A blue-black result indicates starch.
lessons.worked: A destarched plant partly covered with opaque material and exposed to light can test light’s role. Only suitable uncovered green regions should accumulate starch, provided other conditions allow photosynthesis.
lessons.question: Give two limitations of counting pondweed bubbles and one way to improve the evidence.
scheme: Bubbles have variable volumes
Some oxygen dissolves or is used in respiration
Collect gas volume over a fixed time and repeat while controlling conditions
lessons.mistake: Bubble counts are a proxy, not a direct count of glucose molecules made.

cards.definition: A measurement used as an indicator of another quantity.
Allowing stored starch in a plant to be used up before an investigation.

quiz.q: Why can oxygen volume be better than bubble count?
opts: Every bubble always has the same size.
quiz.why: Counting bubbles treats unequal bubbles as equal; a collected volume measures gas more directly.

misconception.q: In this lesson on pondweed, starch tests and evaluating photosynthesis evidence, Sam says: “Every bubble always has the same size.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Bubbles can have different volumes.
Counting bubbles treats unequal bubbles as equal; a collected volume measures gas more directly.

lessons.title: Investigation: candle burning and air volume
notes: A candle flame requires fuel, oxygen and sufficient energy to maintain combustion. Covering it with a container changes its access to fresh air. A simple relationship between container volume and burning time is a model with limitations.

Compare container volumes while controlling candle, wick length, initial conditions and placement. Time a clearly defined endpoint, repeat and graph volume against mean burning time. Hot glass and flames need a supervised risk assessment.
lessons.worked: Larger air volumes may support longer burning, but the flame can extinguish before every oxygen molecule is used. Changes in gas composition and heat losses also influence the outcome.
lessons.question: Identify variables for testing how container volume affects candle burning time.
scheme: Independent: container air volume
Dependent: time until extinction
Control candle/wick, initial conditions and timing rule
lessons.mistake: Do not conclude that an extinguished candle proves all oxygen is gone.

cards.definition: The factor deliberately changed.
A clearly defined event used to finish a measurement.

quiz.q: What should be controlled in an air-volume candle investigation?
opts: The time to extinction being measured.
quiz.why: Control the fuel and starting conditions so container volume is the intended difference.

misconception.q: In this lesson on investigation: candle burning and air volume, Sam says: “The container volume being tested.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Candle and wick conditions.
Control the fuel and starting conditions so container volume is the intended difference.

lessons.title: Investigation: bouncing balls
notes: A falling ball transfers gravitational energy to kinetic energy. Impact can store energy elastically and dissipate some into thermal stores and sound. Rebound height depends on the ball, surface and conditions.

Change ball type while controlling release height, surface and release technique, then measure the maximum rebound height. Repeat trials and compare means and spread. Video against a scale can reduce reading difficulty.
lessons.worked: For a fixed ball mass, a rebound to 60% of drop height corresponds approximately to retaining 60% of its gravitational energy at the top, assuming the same reference level and negligible size effects.
lessons.question: Explain why rebound height is usually lower than drop height and how to make a fair comparison of two balls.
scheme: Some energy is dissipated to surroundings
Keep release height and surface constant
Repeat and measure rebound height consistently
lessons.mistake: Energy is conserved overall even though useful mechanical energy decreases.

cards.definition: The maximum height reached after a bounce.
Transfer of energy into less useful stores in the surroundings.

quiz.q: Why is a rebound usually lower than the drop height?
opts: Gravity switches off after the bounce.
quiz.why: Energy transfers to thermal stores and sound, so less remains for the rebound.

misconception.q: In this lesson on investigation: bouncing balls, Sam says: “Energy is destroyed at impact.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Some mechanical energy is dissipated.
Energy transfers to thermal stores and sound, so less remains for the rebound.

lessons.title: Investigation: bungee extension and safe clearance
notes: A hanging mass has weight and stretches an elastic cord. Extension is stretched length minus original length. Elastic behaviour depends on the material and need not remain proportional over all loads.

Change mass systematically and measure extension after settling. Control cord length and material, use modest supervised loads and provide clearance. Plot force against extension, using W=mg where appropriate, and do not extrapolate an unsafe maximum.
lessons.worked: A cord originally 20 cm long reaching 27 cm has extension 7 cm. Another load producing length 30 cm gives extension 10 cm, not 30 cm.
lessons.question: State how to measure extension and give two controls in a bungee investigation.
scheme: Subtract original length from stretched length
Use the same cord/material/original length
Keep measurement position and settling/timing procedure consistent
lessons.mistake: Elastic cords do not necessarily follow a straight-line force–extension relationship.

cards.definition: Stretched length minus original length.
A change of shape reversed when the force is removed.

quiz.q: A cord lengthens from 20 cm to 28 cm. What is its extension?
quiz.why: Extension measures the increase in length, not the full stretched length.

misconception.q: In this lesson on investigation: bungee extension and safe clearance, Sam says: “28 cm.” Explain the mistake.
ms: 8 cm.
Extension measures the increase in length, not the full stretched length.

lessons.title: Investigation: conduction through metals
notes: Thermal conduction transfers energy through particle interactions, with mobile electrons contributing in metals. Comparing conductors requires controlling their dimensions and heating conditions.

Use rods of matching length and cross-section with the same heat source. A supervised indicator such as wax melting can show energy transfer, but endpoint judgement and contact differences create uncertainty. Repeat rather than relying on one result.
lessons.worked: If a wax marker melts earlier on one otherwise comparable rod, that rod may transfer thermal energy faster. A thicker rod or stronger heating could also explain a shorter time, so control them.
lessons.question: Explain two controls needed to compare thermal conduction in metal rods.
scheme: Same length and cross-sectional area
Same heating arrangement/starting temperature
Link controls to avoiding alternative explanations
lessons.mistake: Faster heating in one setup does not prove material type was the only cause.

cards.definition: A material through which thermal energy transfers readily.
A comparison controlling other factors that could affect the result.

quiz.q: What is essential when comparing metal rods?
opts: A different flame for each rod.
Changing rod length together with metal type.
quiz.why: Geometry and heating affect transfer, so uncontrolled changes could explain the result.

misconception.q: In this lesson on investigation: conduction through metals, Sam says: “A different flame for each rod.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Matching dimensions and heating conditions.
Geometry and heating affect transfer, so uncontrolled changes could explain the result.

lessons.title: Investigation: paper cases and falling motion
notes: Nested paper cupcake cases can model how weight and drag affect a fall. More cases increase mass with a similar shape, although geometry and airflow may also change. Terminal speed occurs when drag balances weight.

Drop from a fixed safe height, release without pushing and measure time using video or repeated timings. Control case type and orientation. State whether the height is sufficient to approach terminal speed; average fall speed alone does not establish it.
lessons.worked: Two nested cases have greater weight than one. They may need a greater falling speed to produce matching drag, but the investigation must check repeatability and shape consistency.
lessons.question: Explain why measuring average falling speed does not prove a paper case reached terminal velocity.
scheme: Average combines changing speeds
Terminal velocity requires constant velocity with balanced forces
Use position–time/video evidence of steady speed
lessons.mistake: The folder name “cupcakes” refers here to falling paper cases, not a baking reaction.

cards.definition: A force opposing motion through a fluid.
Constant velocity when weight and resistive forces balance.

quiz.q: Does one average falling speed prove terminal velocity was reached?
opts: No; it can combine changing speeds.
Yes; every falling object is always at terminal velocity.
Yes; time measurements show forces are zero.
quiz.why: Evidence of a constant speed over part of the fall is needed.

misconception.q: In this lesson on investigation: paper cases and falling motion, Sam says: “Yes; every falling object is always at terminal velocity.” Explain the mistake.
ms: No; it can combine changing speeds.
Evidence of a constant speed over part of the fall is needed.

lessons.title: Investigation: salt amount and dissolving time
notes: Dissolving rate depends on conditions including temperature, agitation, particle size and concentration. Solubility limits the amount that can dissolve at a stated temperature. Adding more solute is not the same experiment as changing solute type.

Change salt mass while controlling water volume, temperature, stirring and grain size. Define the endpoint consistently and note any mass that does not fully dissolve. Do not record “longer time” indefinitely for a saturated solution.
lessons.worked: Increasing mass may lengthen the time to dissolve fully, while at sufficiently high mass some salt remains. That is evidence of saturation under those conditions, rather than a failed stopwatch.
lessons.question: Explain why a dissolving-time investigation becomes difficult once the solution is saturated.
scheme: Maximum soluble amount has been reached at those conditions
Undissolved salt remains
A finite time to complete dissolving is no longer a suitable endpoint
lessons.mistake: Solubility and dissolving rate are different quantities.

cards.definition: Maximum amount dissolving in a given solvent amount at stated conditions.
How quickly a solute dissolves.

quiz.q: What happens if too much salt is added to a saturated solution?
opts: It must all dissolve given the same conditions.
quiz.why: At a fixed temperature and solvent amount, the maximum soluble amount has been reached.

misconception.q: In this lesson on investigation: salt amount and dissolving time, Sam says: “It must all dissolve given the same conditions.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Some remains undissolved.
At a fixed temperature and solvent amount, the maximum soluble amount has been reached.

lessons.title: Investigation: temperature and diffusion
notes: Particles move randomly and their average kinetic energy increases with temperature. A colour-spreading experiment can model diffusion, but bulk water movement can also transport colour.

Change temperature while controlling liquid volume, dye amount, vessel dimensions and starting position. Avoid stirring and let water settle. Record a defined colour boundary or time to an agreed endpoint, repeat and evaluate convection as a confounding factor.
lessons.worked: Dye may spread faster in warm water, but uneven heating can create convection currents. A cautious conclusion distinguishes the observed pattern from proof that diffusion alone caused all visible movement.
lessons.question: Suggest two controls and one limitation when comparing colour spreading in warm and cool water.
scheme: Same vessel/water volume/dye amount
Avoid stirring and use the same release method
Convection or subjective boundary judgement can affect results
lessons.mistake: Visible spreading can involve convection as well as molecular diffusion.

cards.definition: Net movement down a concentration gradient due to random motion.
Energy and material transfer by bulk movement in a fluid.

quiz.q: What can confound a warm-water dye-spreading experiment?
quiz.why: Bulk movement can carry dye, so visible spreading is not necessarily due to diffusion alone.

misconception.q: In this lesson on investigation: temperature and diffusion, Sam says: “Keeping dye amount the same.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Convection currents.
Bulk movement can carry dye, so visible spreading is not necessarily due to diffusion alone.

lessons.title: Permanent magnets, fields and the Earth
notes: A permanent magnet has north- and south-seeking poles. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. A magnetic field is a region where a magnetic material or magnet experiences a force. Iron, nickel, cobalt and some alloys are magnetic.

Outside a bar magnet field lines run north to south; closer spacing indicates a stronger field. A compass’s north-seeking end points roughly towards geographic north because the Earth’s field there behaves broadly like a magnetic south pole.
lessons.worked: A compass aligns with the local field. An unmagnetised iron object can be attracted near either pole because it becomes induced magnetically; attraction alone does not prove an object is a permanent magnet.
lessons.question: Explain why attraction alone cannot show that a metal object is a permanent magnet.
scheme: A magnetic material can be induced by a nearby magnet
It can then be attracted
Repulsion provides stronger evidence that the tested object is itself a magnet
lessons.mistake: The north-seeking end of a compass is its north pole, not its south pole.

cards.definition: A region where a magnet or magnetic material experiences a force.
A material becoming magnetised in a nearby magnetic field.

quiz.q: Which is stronger evidence that an object is itself a magnet?
opts: It is attracted to a magnet.
It repels a known magnet in one orientation.
quiz.why: Induced magnetic materials can be attracted; repulsion indicates interacting magnetic poles.

misconception.q: In this lesson on permanent magnets, fields and the earth, Sam says: “It is attracted to a magnet.” Explain the mistake.
ms: It repels a known magnet in one orientation.
Induced magnetic materials can be attracted; repulsion indicates interacting magnetic poles.

lessons.title: Electromagnets, relays and fair comparisons
notes: A current creates a magnetic field. A coil concentrates the field, and an iron core can increase it. An electromagnet can be switched and its strength changed by changing current, turns or core conditions.

Compare one factor at a time; increasing turns may also change resistance and current, so monitor current if it must be controlled. Avoid overheating coils. Relays use an electromagnet to operate a switch; scrapyard magnets release loads when current is removed.
lessons.worked: In a relay a small control current magnetises a coil, attracts an armature and closes another circuit. The mechanical switching separates the control action from the load circuit.
lessons.question: Describe two ways to increase an electromagnet’s strength and one control for a fair test of coil turns.
scheme: Increase current
Add turns or an appropriate iron core
For a turns comparison keep core/geometry consistent and monitor/control current
lessons.mistake: A current-carrying coil produces a field even without an iron core.

cards.definition: A magnet produced by current in a coil.
A switch operated by an electromagnet.

quiz.q: How can an electromagnet be strengthened?
opts: Increase the current under suitable safe conditions.
quiz.why: A larger coil current increases its magnetic field; turns and core also matter.

misconception.q: In this lesson on electromagnets, relays and fair comparisons, Sam says: “Remove every coil turn.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Increase the current under suitable safe conditions.
A larger coil current increases its magnetic field; turns and core also matter.

lessons.title: Plan fair tests, measurements and repeats
notes: A method must say what to do, what to measure, the units, the range and how to reduce risks. Resolution is the smallest detectable change. Accuracy concerns closeness to the true value; precision concerns the spread of repeated values.

Choose equipment with suitable range and resolution, check zero readings, repeat each condition and calculate a mean when appropriate. Repeatability uses the same method and setup; reproducibility compares different people or equipment.
lessons.worked: Timing ten oscillations and dividing by ten reduces the fractional effect of reaction time compared with timing just one. Repeating reduces random variation but cannot remove a miscalibrated clock.
lessons.question: Explain two ways to improve a measurement of the time for one pendulum swing.
scheme: Time several swings and divide by their number
Repeat and calculate a mean
Use the same start/finish position and small release angle
lessons.mistake: Repeated measurements do not fix a systematic offset.

cards.definition: The smallest change an instrument can detect.
Agreement when the same person repeats a method with the same equipment.

quiz.q: Why time ten swings instead of just one?
opts: Reaction time has a smaller fractional effect.
It makes the clock perfectly accurate.
quiz.why: The timing interval is longer, so the same reaction-time delay is a smaller fraction of it.

misconception.q: In this lesson on plan fair tests, measurements and repeats, Sam says: “It removes all systematic errors.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Reaction time has a smaller fractional effect.
The timing interval is longer, so the same reaction-time delay is a smaller fraction of it.

lessons.title: Work done and simple machines
notes: Work is energy transferred by a force moving an object through a distance in the force’s direction: W=Fs. Work is measured in joules. A machine can reduce required force by increasing the distance through which that force acts.

Identify the relevant distance and direction, convert units and multiply. In an ideal machine, input work equals useful output work; real machines dissipate some energy. A lever or pulley does not create energy.
lessons.worked: A 40 N force acting over 3 m does 120 J of work. An ideal pulley that halves lifting force requires twice the pulling distance for the same lifted height.
lessons.question: Calculate work done by a 25 N force moving an object 4 m in the force’s direction, and explain why a machine cannot create extra energy.
scheme: W=Fs
Energy is conserved; reduced force trades against increased input distance in an ideal machine
lessons.mistake: A large force with no movement does no mechanical work on that stationary object.

cards.definition: Energy transferred by a force moving an object through a distance in its direction.
A device trading force against movement distance.

quiz.q: An ideal pulley halves the lifting force. What is the trade-off?
opts: Twice the input pulling distance for the same lifted height.
quiz.why: Input work equals useful output work in the ideal model, so force × distance stays consistent.

misconception.q: In this lesson on work done and simple machines, Sam says: “Free extra energy.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Twice the input pulling distance for the same lifted height.
Input work equals useful output work in the ideal model, so force × distance stays consistent.

lessons.title: Food energy and evaluating heating experiments
notes: Food contains chemical energy. Burning a food sample can transfer energy by heating to water, but a classroom setup captures only part of the food’s energy. Compare energy per gram when masses differ.

Control water volume, starting temperature and apparatus spacing. Measure the mass burned and temperature rise. Energy can escape to air or heat apparatus; incomplete burning also makes a food comparison less reliable.
lessons.worked: If a smaller food mass heats the same water through a greater temperature rise, it may supply more captured energy per gram. This conclusion is limited unless energy losses and burning completeness are comparable.
lessons.question: Give two limitations of comparing foods by burning them beneath a tube of water.
scheme: Energy escapes to surroundings rather than all heating the water
Incomplete combustion or unequal burning changes captured energy
Control water mass and compare energy per gram
lessons.mistake: A temperature rise alone cannot compare energy content when sample masses differ.

cards.definition: Energy associated with the chemical arrangement of substances.
Energy divided by the mass of material involved.

quiz.q: Why compare food energy per gram?
opts: Every food sample has the same energy.
Food samples may have different masses.
A temperature rise is always the full food energy.
quiz.why: A fair comparison accounts for sample mass and limitations such as heat loss.

misconception.q: In this lesson on food energy and evaluating heating experiments, Sam says: “A temperature rise is always the full food energy.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Food samples may have different masses.
A fair comparison accounts for sample mass and limitations such as heat loss.

lessons.title: Levers, turning effects and moments
notes: A moment is a force’s turning effect around a pivot. Moment=force×perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action, measured in N m. A lever can increase a turning effect by increasing this distance.

For rotational equilibrium total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment. Use perpendicular distances, not an arbitrary length to the force application point. Balance of moments alone does not guarantee zero resultant force.
lessons.worked: A 20 N force at 0.3 m gives moment 6 N m. To balance it with an opposite force at 0.6 m requires 10 N, because 10×0.6=6.
lessons.question: A 12 N force acts 0.5 m from a pivot. What opposing force at 0.3 m balances the moment?
scheme: Moment 12×0.5=6 N m
Opposing force satisfies F×0.3=6
F=20 N
lessons.mistake: The distance is perpendicular to the force’s line of action.

cards.definition: The turning effect of a force about a pivot.
The point or axis about which turning occurs.

quiz.q: Which distance is used to calculate a moment?
opts: Perpendicular distance to the force’s line of action.
Any diagonal distance to the load.
The total length of the object.
quiz.why: The effective lever arm is perpendicular to the line of action.

misconception.q: In this lesson on levers, turning effects and moments, Sam says: “Any diagonal distance to the load.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Perpendicular distance to the force’s line of action.
The effective lever arm is perpendicular to the line of action.

lessons.title: Temperature, energy and conduction
notes: Temperature relates to average particle kinetic energy; an object’s thermal store also depends on how much material it contains and what it is. Energy transfers spontaneously from hotter to cooler regions.

Conduction transfers energy through particle interactions without bulk material flow. In metals mobile electrons also help transfer energy. A large cooler bath may contain more thermal energy than a small hotter cup, depending on the reference comparison.
lessons.worked: A metal spoon handle warms when its other end is in hot water because energy spreads through the metal. The metal atoms do not travel from the water to the handle.
lessons.question: Explain why temperature alone cannot compare the thermal stores of a cup of water and a bath.
scheme: Temperature relates to average particle energy
The bath contains much more material
Total energy also depends on mass and material
lessons.mistake: Heat is an energy transfer, not a substance stored in objects.

cards.definition: A measure related to average particle kinetic energy.
Thermal energy transfer through interactions without bulk flow.

quiz.q: Does a hotter small cup necessarily have a larger thermal store than a cooler bath?
opts: Yes; temperature alone decides the total store.
No; mass and material also matter.
quiz.why: Total thermal energy depends on the amount of material as well as temperature.

misconception.q: In this lesson on temperature, energy and conduction, Sam says: “Yes; temperature alone decides the total store.” Explain the mistake.
ms: No; mass and material also matter.
Total thermal energy depends on the amount of material as well as temperature.

lessons.title: Convection, radiation and insulation
notes: Convection involves bulk movement in fluids: warmer, less dense regions can rise while cooler denser regions sink in a gravitational field. Thermal radiation is electromagnetic transfer and can cross a vacuum.

Insulation reduces transfer pathways. Trapped air reduces conduction and limits convection; shiny low-emissivity surfaces reduce thermal radiation. A vacuum reduces conduction and convection but does not prevent radiation.
lessons.worked: A vacuum flask uses a vacuum gap to reduce conduction and convection, reflective surfaces to reduce radiation and an insulated stopper to limit other transfers. No real flask completely prevents energy transfer.
lessons.question: Explain how trapped air and a shiny surface can help insulation.
scheme: Air is a poor conductor
Small pockets limit convection
Shiny surfaces have low emissivity and reduce thermal radiation
lessons.mistake: Warm fluid rises due to density differences; “heat rises” is not a complete explanation.

cards.definition: Transfer by bulk movement of a fluid.
Energy transfer by electromagnetic radiation.
A material or arrangement that reduces a transfer pathway.

quiz.q: Which transfer can cross a vacuum?
quiz.why: Electromagnetic radiation needs no material medium; conduction and convection do.

misconception.q: In this lesson on convection, radiation and insulation, Sam says: “Convection across the vacuum.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Thermal radiation.
Electromagnetic radiation needs no material medium; conduction and convection do.

lessons.title: The atmosphere and carbon cycle
notes: Dry air near Earth’s surface is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and about 1% other gases. Water vapour varies. Carbon moves between atmosphere, organisms, oceans and rocks through several processes.

Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide, while respiration, combustion and decomposition return carbon to the environment. Long-term burial stores carbon; burning fossil fuels transfers stored carbon into the atmosphere on much shorter timescales.
lessons.worked: A growing tree takes in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis and incorporates carbon into organic material. Cutting and burning the tree returns much of that carbon, so a full carbon accounting must consider both uptake and release.
lessons.question: Name two processes that add carbon dioxide to air and one that removes it.
scheme: Respiration
Combustion or decomposition
Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide
lessons.mistake: The carbon cycle tracks carbon atoms, not a one-way journey of energy.

cards.definition: The gases surrounding a planet.
Movement of carbon through organisms and the physical environment.

quiz.q: Which process removes carbon dioxide from air?
quiz.why: Photosynthesis incorporates carbon into organic substances; combustion and respiration return it.

misconception.q: In this lesson on the atmosphere and carbon cycle, Sam says: “Burning fossil fuels.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis incorporates carbon into organic substances; combustion and respiration return it.

lessons.title: Greenhouse effect, climate evidence and human activity
notes: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, influencing the balance between incoming solar energy and outgoing radiation. The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warmer than it would otherwise be. Human activities increase some greenhouse-gas concentrations.

Burning fossil fuels, land-use change and some agricultural processes contribute. Distinguish weather over short periods from climate patterns over decades. Evaluate long-term data and multiple evidence sources, not one cold day or one local record.
lessons.worked: Increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide changes the outgoing energy balance and contributes to warming. Consequences can include sea-level rise, altered weather patterns and ecosystem changes; local effects vary.
lessons.question: Explain how increased carbon dioxide can contribute to global warming.
scheme: Carbon dioxide absorbs outgoing infrared radiation
It re-emits radiation and changes net energy loss
A higher equilibrium temperature is reached under the changed energy balance
lessons.mistake: The greenhouse effect is not primarily a hole in the ozone layer.

cards.definition: A gas absorbing and re-emitting infrared radiation.
Patterns in weather over long periods.

quiz.q: What is central to the enhanced greenhouse effect?
opts: A hole allowing extra visible sunlight through.
One cold day disproving a long-term trend.
Changed absorption and re-emission of outgoing infrared.
quiz.why: Increasing greenhouse gases changes Earth’s energy balance and contributes to warming.

misconception.q: In this lesson on greenhouse effect, climate evidence and human activity, Sam says: “A hole allowing extra visible sunlight through.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Changed absorption and re-emission of outgoing infrared.
Increasing greenhouse gases changes Earth’s energy balance and contributes to warming.

lessons.title: Metal extraction, displacement and resources
notes: An ore contains enough of a useful substance for extraction to be worthwhile under the conditions. A metal’s reactivity influences extraction: carbon can reduce oxides of some metals below carbon in the reactivity series; more reactive metals commonly require electrolysis.

Separate a general rule from specific conditions and economics. Displacement provides evidence of relative reactivity. Finite deposits, energy needs, pollution and transport all affect the costs of using metals.
lessons.worked: Iron oxide can be reduced using carbon-based processes because iron is below carbon in the series. Aluminium is more reactive and industrial extraction uses electrolysis of suitable molten compounds.
lessons.question: Explain why carbon reduction works for some metal oxides but not for aluminium oxide under ordinary extraction conditions.
scheme: Carbon can displace/reduce metals less reactive than itself
Aluminium is above carbon
Aluminium extraction therefore requires a different process such as electrolysis
lessons.mistake: Being common in rocks does not mean an element is easy to extract.

cards.definition: A material containing enough useful substance for extraction to be worthwhile.
Here, removal of oxygen from a metal oxide.

quiz.q: Why is aluminium not normally extracted using carbon reduction?
opts: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon.
quiz.why: Carbon reduces oxides of suitable metals below it in the reactivity series.

misconception.q: In this lesson on metal extraction, displacement and resources, Sam says: “Aluminium contains no atoms.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon.
Carbon reduces oxides of suitable metals below it in the reactivity series.

lessons.title: Metal properties, oxidation and reactivity
notes: Metals typically conduct electricity and heat and can be shaped; non-metals have varied properties and important exceptions, such as conducting graphite. Metal + oxygen commonly forms a metal oxide.

A reactivity series compares tendencies to react. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a suitable compound in solution. Evaluate actual observations and conditions rather than assuming every metal reacts visibly with water.
lessons.worked: Iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper. Iron is more reactive than copper, so copper is deposited. Copper cannot displace iron from iron sulfate solution.
lessons.question: Predict whether zinc displaces copper from copper sulfate and explain why, given zinc is more reactive.
scheme: Zinc displaces copper
Zinc is more reactive
Products are zinc sulfate and copper
lessons.mistake: Not every metal is magnetic and not every non-metal is an electrical insulator.

cards.definition: A reaction in which a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one in a compound.
At this level, a reaction in which a substance gains oxygen.

quiz.q: Can copper displace iron from iron sulfate, if iron is more reactive?
opts: Yes, because all metals displace each other.
quiz.why: A metal displaces another only when it is more reactive under the stated conditions.

misconception.q: In this lesson on metal properties, oxidation and reactivity, Sam says: “Yes, because all metals displace each other.” Explain the mistake.
ms: No.
A metal displaces another only when it is more reactive under the stated conditions.

lessons.title: Recycling and life-cycle evaluation
