notes: Reusing keeps a product in service; recycling processes materials into new products. Both can conserve resources, but impacts depend on collection, sorting, energy use, transport and product quality.

Compare a whole life cycle: extraction, manufacture, use and disposal. Use numerical data if supplied and state trade-offs. A claim of “recyclable” does not mean that every local system can or does recycle the item.
lessons.worked: Recycling aluminium usually avoids much of the energy-intensive ore extraction stage. Contamination and mixed materials can add sorting costs, so design for separation may improve practical recovery.
lessons.question: Give two benefits and one limitation of metal recycling.
scheme: Conserves finite ore/resources
Can reduce extraction energy and associated impacts
Collection, contamination or processing requires resources
lessons.mistake: Recycling is beneficial in many cases but not a process with zero energy use.

cards.definition: Using a product again without converting its material into a new material product.
Processing recovered materials into new products.
Stages from extraction through production and use to disposal.

quiz.q: Which is a sound recycling evaluation?
opts: Compare resources and energy across the life cycle.
quiz.why: Benefits can be substantial, but processing, collection and sorting still have impacts.

misconception.q: In this lesson on recycling and life-cycle evaluation, Sam says: “Assume recycling needs no energy.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Compare resources and energy across the life cycle.
Benefits can be substantial, but processing, collection and sorting still have impacts.

lessons.title: Evolution by natural selection
notes: Individuals in a population vary, and some variation is inherited. When a trait improves survival and reproduction in a particular environment, the alleles associated with it can become more frequent over generations.

Describe variation first, then the environmental selection pressure, differential reproduction and inheritance. Mutations do not arise because an organism needs a particular change. Individuals do not deliberately evolve; population characteristics change over generations.
lessons.worked: If a dry habitat favours a heritable water-saving feature, individuals carrying it may leave more offspring. Over many generations that feature can become more common without any conscious choice.
lessons.question: Explain natural selection when an inherited trait improves survival in a changed environment.
scheme: Inherited variation already exists
Individuals with an advantageous trait tend to survive/reproduce more
Offspring inherit associated alleles, changing their frequency over generations
lessons.mistake: Survival alone is not enough; reproduction and inheritance link the generations.

cards.definition: Change in inherited trait frequencies through differences in survival and reproduction.
Differences linked to genetic information passed between generations.

quiz.q: Which is needed for natural selection to change a population?
opts: Individuals choosing which mutations they need.
Every individual surviving equally with no inherited variation.
quiz.why: Differences must connect to inheritance and reproductive success across generations.

misconception.q: In this lesson on evolution by natural selection, Sam says: “Individuals choosing which mutations they need.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Inherited differences affecting reproduction.
Differences must connect to inheritance and reproductive success across generations.

lessons.title: Darwin, competing ideas and evidence
notes: Darwin and Wallace developed explanations of evolution through natural selection. Scientific ideas are assessed using evidence and can be refined. Fossils, similarities between organisms and genetic evidence support change and common ancestry.

Distinguish a well-supported scientific theory from an untested guess. Acquired changes such as a trained muscle are not automatically inherited. Modern genetics explains inheritance in ways that were unavailable to early evolution researchers.
lessons.worked: A giraffe does not genetically lengthen its offspring’s neck simply by stretching. In a natural-selection model, inherited differences affect reproductive success, and population frequencies change over generations.
lessons.question: Explain why stretching a muscle during life is not the same process as inherited evolution.
scheme: It is an acquired individual change
It need not alter inherited genetic information
Evolution involves inherited population changes across generations
lessons.mistake: A scientific theory is an explanatory framework supported and tested by evidence.

cards.definition: A tested explanatory framework supported by evidence.
A feature developed during an individual’s lifetime.

quiz.q: Why is muscle training not itself inherited evolution?
opts: An acquired change need not alter inherited genetic information.
Every acquired trait is automatically inherited.
quiz.why: Evolution concerns inherited population changes across generations.

misconception.q: In this lesson on darwin, competing ideas and evidence, Sam says: “Every acquired trait is automatically inherited.” Explain the mistake.
ms: An acquired change need not alter inherited genetic information.
Evolution concerns inherited population changes across generations.

lessons.title: Extinction, endangered species and biodiversity
notes: Extinction occurs when a species has no living individuals left. Risk can increase through habitat loss, environmental change, disease, invasive species or overexploitation. Biodiversity includes the variety of species and genetic diversity within them.

Conservation can protect habitats, reduce pressures and maintain breeding populations. Captive breeding or seed banks can help but do not automatically restore a functioning ecosystem. Evaluate evidence and the reason a particular intervention addresses the threat.
lessons.worked: Protecting a breeding habitat can support food, shelter and reproduction at once. A breeding programme without suitable habitat for release may preserve individuals but not a self-sustaining wild population.
lessons.question: Explain one habitat-based conservation method and one limitation of captive breeding alone.
scheme: Protect/restore habitat to support survival and reproduction
Captive breeding may maintain numbers/genetic stock
Without suitable wild habitat, release may not sustain a population
lessons.mistake: Endangered means at risk of extinction, not already extinct.

cards.definition: The variety of life, including species and genetic diversity.
Loss of all living members of a species.
Actions protecting species, habitats and biodiversity.

quiz.q: Why may captive breeding alone fail to restore a species?
opts: Suitable wild habitat and reduced threats are also needed.
quiz.why: A self-sustaining wild population needs conditions supporting survival and reproduction.

misconception.q: In this lesson on extinction, endangered species and biodiversity, Sam says: “Breeding automatically removes every threat.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Suitable wild habitat and reduced threats are also needed.
A self-sustaining wild population needs conditions supporting survival and reproduction.

lessons.title: DNA, genes, chromosomes and inherited variation
notes: DNA carries genetic information. A gene is a section of DNA that contributes to a functional product; different versions are alleles. Chromosomes are long DNA molecules associated with proteins. Most human body cells have chromosomes in pairs.

Gametes carry one chromosome from each pair, and fertilisation restores pairs. Many traits depend on several genes and the environment. A mutation is a change in DNA and may be harmful, neutral or beneficial depending on context.
lessons.worked: A child inherits genetic material from both biological parents, but is not an exact average of their visible characteristics. New combinations of alleles contribute to variation.
lessons.question: Explain the relationship between DNA, genes and chromosomes.
scheme: Chromosomes contain long DNA molecules
Genes are sections of DNA
Alleles are alternative versions of a gene
lessons.mistake: Dominant does not mean more common, stronger or better.

cards.definition: A section of DNA contributing to a functional product.
An alternative version of a gene.
A long DNA molecule associated with proteins.

quiz.q: What is an allele?
quiz.why: Different versions of a gene can contribute to inherited variation.

misconception.q: In this lesson on dna, genes, chromosomes and inherited variation, Sam says: “An entire organism.” Explain the mistake.
ms: A version of a gene.
Different versions of a gene can contribute to inherited variation.

lessons.title: DNA evidence, structure and extraction
notes: DNA has a double-helix structure. Models of its structure were developed using multiple lines of evidence and contributions from several researchers, including Franklin, Wilkins, Watson and Crick. A classroom extraction makes DNA-rich material visible but does not reveal its molecular structure.

In a supervised fruit extraction, detergent disrupts membranes, salt can help DNA aggregate and cold ethanol helps precipitate DNA. Keep ethanol away from flames and do not taste materials. The visible strands contain many molecules and may include impurities.
lessons.worked: A white precipitate in an extraction is consistent with DNA-rich material from many cells. Seeing it does not show the sequence of bases, prove sample purity or reveal individual genes by eye.
lessons.question: Explain the roles of detergent and ethanol in a classroom DNA extraction.
scheme: Detergent disrupts lipid membranes
DNA is released from cells/nuclei
Ethanol reduces DNA solubility so DNA-rich material precipitates
lessons.mistake: Visible strands are not a magnified view of one double helix.

cards.definition: The molecule carrying genetic information.
A solid that separates from a solution.

quiz.q: What do visible strands in a classroom DNA extraction show?
opts: DNA-rich material from many molecules, potentially with impurities.
The exact base sequence by eye.
A complete view of one individual gene.
quiz.why: The extraction makes aggregated material visible; it does not resolve the molecular sequence.

misconception.q: In this lesson on dna evidence, structure and extraction, Sam says: “The exact base sequence by eye.” Explain the mistake.
ms: DNA-rich material from many molecules, potentially with impurities.
The extraction makes aggregated material visible; it does not resolve the molecular sequence.

lessons.title: Genetic crosses and probability
notes: For a simple single-gene model, a dominant allele is expressed with one copy, while a recessive phenotype requires two recessive copies. Genotype names the allele combination; phenotype is the expressed characteristic.

Write parental genotypes and possible gametes, then combine them in a Punnett square. State the model assumptions. Each offspring is a new probabilistic event: a 1-in-4 chance does not require exactly one in every four siblings.
lessons.worked: For Aa×Aa, combinations are AA, Aa, Aa, aa. Genotype ratio is 1:2:1; with complete dominance the phenotype ratio is 3:1. Use a hypothetical trait rather than claiming that all real human traits fit it.
lessons.question: In a simple dominant/recessive model, cross Aa with aa and find the chance of the recessive phenotype.
scheme: Gametes A or a from Aa and a from aa
Offspring Aa or aa in equal probability
Recessive phenotype probability 1/2 or 50%
lessons.mistake: A Punnett square predicts probabilities, not a guaranteed family sequence.

cards.definition: The allele combination for a gene or genes.
An expressed characteristic.
An allele whose phenotype in a simple complete-dominance model needs two copies.

quiz.q: For Aa × Aa in a simple complete-dominance model, what is P(aa)?
opts: Exactly one in every four siblings.
quiz.why: Each offspring has an independent one-in-four chance; a family need not match the ratio exactly.

misconception.q: In this lesson on genetic crosses and probability, Sam says: “Exactly one in every four siblings.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Each offspring has an independent one-in-four chance; a family need not match the ratio exactly.

lessons.title: Genetic modification: benefits and limitations
notes: Genetic modification changes an organism’s genetic material using biotechnology. It can introduce or alter a trait, but the effect depends on the gene, organism and environment. Selective breeding instead chooses parents with desired inherited traits over generations.

Evaluate a specific use with evidence. Possible benefits include producing medicines or reducing crop damage; concerns can involve ecological effects, access, resistance and unintended consequences. Do not assume all applications have identical risks or benefits.
lessons.worked: Bacteria can be engineered to produce human insulin under controlled industrial conditions. A crop altered for pest resistance poses a different evaluation involving farming systems and effects on other organisms.
lessons.question: Distinguish genetic modification from selective breeding and give a potential benefit of one named use.
scheme: GM directly changes genetic material using biotechnology
Selective breeding chooses parents over generations
A specific justified benefit, such as producing insulin
lessons.mistake: A judgement should concern a particular application, rather than treating every modified organism as identical.

cards.definition: Changing genetic material using biotechnology.
Choosing parents with desired inherited traits over generations.

quiz.q: How does selective breeding differ from genetic modification?
opts: It chooses parents rather than directly editing genetic material.
quiz.why: Selecting parents changes inherited combinations over generations, using a different method from direct modification.

misconception.q: In this lesson on genetic modification: benefits and limitations, Sam says: “It changes every individual instantly.” Explain the mistake.
ms: It chooses parents rather than directly editing genetic material.
Selecting parents changes inherited combinations over generations, using a different method from direct modification.

lessons.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves
notes: A transverse wave oscillates perpendicular to energy transfer; a longitudinal wave oscillates parallel. Amplitude is maximum displacement, wavelength is spacing between corresponding points and frequency counts complete oscillations each second.
Wave speed=f×λ and period=1/f. Distinguish a moving wave pattern from the local oscillation of material. Electromagnetic waves do not need a material medium, whereas sound does.
lessons.worked: A wave of frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 0.8 m has speed 4 m/s and period 0.2 s. A larger amplitude does not necessarily change the speed in the same linear medium.
lessons.question: A wave has frequency 4 Hz and wavelength 1.5 m. Calculate speed and period.
scheme: v=fλ=6 m/s
T=1/f
lessons.mistake: Wavelength is not the distance a particle moves during one oscillation.

cards.definition: A wave with oscillations perpendicular to energy transfer.
Spacing between corresponding points on a wave.
Time for one complete oscillation.

quiz.q: A wave has f=3 Hz and wavelength 2 m. What is its speed?
quiz.why: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength = 3 × 2 = 6 m/s.

misconception.q: In this lesson on transverse and longitudinal waves, Sam says: “1.5 m/s.” Explain the mistake.
ms: 6 m/s.
Wave speed = frequency × wavelength = 3 × 2 = 6 m/s.

lessons.title: Ultrasound and echo applications
notes: Ultrasound is sound at frequencies above about 20 kHz, beyond the typical upper limit of young human hearing. It remains a mechanical wave and needs a medium. Reflections occur at boundaries where acoustic properties change.

Time-of-flight measurements can estimate distances using speed×time/2 for a reflected pulse. Medical imaging uses returning signals to build a picture; gel improves coupling by reducing air gaps. Cleaning uses physical effects in a liquid.
lessons.worked: A pulse returning after 0.00004 s in tissue at 1500 m/s travels 0.06 m in total, so the reflecting boundary is 0.03 m deep. This is a simplified travel-time model.
lessons.question: Explain why a reflected ultrasound distance calculation divides speed×time by two.
scheme: Recorded time includes outward and return journeys
Speed×time gives total path length
Depth is half for a direct reflected path
lessons.mistake: Ultrasound is not an electromagnetic or ionising wave.

cards.definition: Sound above about 20 kHz.
The travel time of a signal over a path.

quiz.q: Can ultrasound cross a vacuum?
opts: Yes; it is an electromagnetic wave.
No; it needs a material medium.
quiz.why: Ultrasound is a mechanical sound wave, despite its high frequency.

misconception.q: In this lesson on ultrasound and echo applications, Sam says: “Yes; it is an electromagnetic wave.” Explain the mistake.
ms: No; it needs a material medium.
Ultrasound is a mechanical sound wave, despite its high frequency.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic waves, uses and ionising radiation
notes: The electromagnetic spectrum is radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma in increasing frequency. Wavelength decreases in that direction. All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.

Uses depend on interactions: radio for communication, infrared for thermal imaging and X-rays for imaging through soft tissue. Higher-energy ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays can ionise matter and damage cells. Risk depends on exposure and the radiation involved.
lessons.worked: X-rays are useful because different tissues absorb them differently. Exposure is controlled to obtain useful information while reducing unnecessary dose. Infrared mainly transfers energy through heating rather than ionisation.
lessons.question: Explain why X-rays can be useful for imaging but require exposure control.
scheme: Different materials/tissues absorb X-rays differently
A detector records the contrast
Ionising radiation can damage cells so exposure is managed
lessons.mistake: All EM waves have the same vacuum speed; higher frequency does not mean faster.

cards.definition: A wave that can transfer energy through a vacuum.
Removal or addition of electrons to form charged particles.

quiz.q: Which EM waves have the same speed in a vacuum?
opts: Only waves with the same frequency.
quiz.why: Their vacuum speed is the same; frequency and wavelength differ.

misconception.q: In this lesson on electromagnetic waves, uses and ionising radiation, Sam says: “Only visible colours.” Explain the mistake.
ms: All of them.
Their vacuum speed is the same; frequency and wavelength differ.

lessons.title: Earth’s layers and rock types
notes: Earth has a thin solid crust, a mantle, a liquid outer core and solid inner core. The mantle is mainly solid rock that deforms slowly over long timescales, rather than a global ocean of liquid magma.

Igneous rocks form when molten material solidifies. Sedimentary rocks form from deposited material that becomes rock, often through compaction and cementation. Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks change under heat and pressure without melting.
lessons.worked: A slowly cooled magma can form large crystals because they have longer to grow. Rapidly cooled lava usually has smaller crystals. Melting a metamorphic rock and cooling it makes an igneous rock.
lessons.question: Compare how igneous and metamorphic rocks form.
scheme: Igneous: molten material cools and solidifies
Metamorphic: existing rock changes with heat/pressure
Metamorphism does not require melting
lessons.mistake: The mantle is largely solid and the outer core is liquid.

cards.definition: The thin outer solid layer of Earth.
The mostly solid rock layer beneath the crust, able to deform slowly.
Rock formed when molten material cools and solidifies.

quiz.q: Which description of Earth is accurate?
opts: The crust is Earth’s thickest layer.
The mantle is mostly solid and the outer core is liquid.
The entire mantle is a liquid magma ocean.
quiz.why: The mantle can flow slowly over geological time without being a global liquid ocean.

misconception.q: In this lesson on earth’s layers and rock types, Sam says: “The entire mantle is a liquid magma ocean.” Explain the mistake.
ms: The mantle is mostly solid and the outer core is liquid.
The mantle can flow slowly over geological time without being a global liquid ocean.

lessons.title: Sedimentary rocks, fossils and weathering
notes: Weathering breaks rock down in place through physical, chemical or biological processes. Erosion transports material. Sediments can be deposited, compacted and cemented into sedimentary rock. Fossils preserve evidence of former organisms.

Freeze–thaw can widen cracks when water freezes and expands. Chemical weathering changes minerals. Fossils commonly form where rapid burial and suitable conditions limit destruction; their record is incomplete and biased.
lessons.worked: A shell buried in fine sediment can leave a fossil as sediment becomes rock. High temperatures during melting or strong metamorphism can destroy evidence, so fossils are usually associated with sedimentary rocks.
lessons.question: Distinguish weathering from erosion and explain why burial can help fossil formation.
scheme: Weathering breaks down rock in place
Erosion moves material
Burial can reduce scavenging/decay and protect remains during preservation
lessons.mistake: The fossil record is incomplete; absence of a fossil does not prove an organism never existed.

cards.definition: Breakdown of rock in place.
Movement of rock material.
Preserved evidence of a former organism.

quiz.q: How does erosion differ from weathering?
quiz.why: Weathering breaks material down where it is; erosion moves it.

misconception.q: In this lesson on sedimentary rocks, fossils and weathering, Sam says: “Erosion must form magma.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Erosion transports material.
Weathering breaks material down where it is; erosion moves it.

lessons.title: The rock cycle and timescales
notes: The rock cycle connects rock types through weathering, erosion, transport, deposition, burial, heat, pressure, melting and cooling. It has multiple pathways and no single required starting point.

Name the actual process on each arrow. Sedimentary rock can metamorphose without melting; any suitable rock can melt and later cool into igneous rock. Uplift and exposure allow renewed weathering over geological timescales.
lessons.worked: An igneous rock exposed at the surface may weather into sediment, become sedimentary rock after burial and cementation, then become metamorphic under increased heat and pressure. Melting is a further distinct step.
lessons.question: Describe a route from sedimentary rock to igneous rock, including the processes.
scheme: Sedimentary rock melts under suitable conditions
Molten material is magma/lava
Cooling and solidification form igneous rock
lessons.mistake: Heat and pressure without melting form metamorphic rock, not automatically igneous rock.

cards.definition: Existing rock changed by heat and pressure without melting.
Connected processes transforming rocks through multiple pathways.

quiz.q: What forms when rock melts and then solidifies?
quiz.why: Cooling molten material forms igneous rock; metamorphism does not require melting.

misconception.q: In this lesson on the rock cycle and timescales, Sam says: “Metamorphic rock without melting.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Igneous rock.
Cooling molten material forms igneous rock; metamorphism does not require melting.

lessons.title: Night sky, Solar System and scale
notes: A star produces radiation through processes including nuclear fusion; a planet or moon is seen mainly by reflected starlight. Our Solar System contains the Sun, planets, moons and smaller bodies. It is part of the Milky Way galaxy.

Distances are huge: an astronomical unit is approximately Earth’s mean Sun distance, and a light-year is a distance light travels in one year. Scale models must preserve ratios; showing both body sizes and orbit distances to one scale is often impractical.
lessons.worked: Neptune is far beyond Earth’s orbit, while the nearest stars are vastly farther away again. A diagram with large visible planets and closely spaced orbits usually uses different scales for size and distance.
lessons.question: Explain what a light-year measures and give one limitation of a typical Solar System classroom diagram.
scheme: Light-year measures distance
Distance travelled by light in one year
Planet sizes and orbit distances are often not shown to a single common scale
lessons.mistake: A light-year is not a unit of time.

cards.definition: The distance light travels in one year.
The Sun and the bodies gravitationally associated with it.
A large system of stars, gas and other matter.

quiz.q: What does a light-year measure?
quiz.why: The word “year” describes the travel interval used to define a very large distance.

misconception.q: In this lesson on night sky, solar system and scale, Sam says: “Time.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Distance.
The word “year” describes the travel interval used to define a very large distance.

lessons.title: Orbits, seasons and eclipses
notes: Gravity continually changes an orbiting body’s direction. Earth rotates approximately once each day and orbits the Sun approximately once each year. Its tilted rotational axis explains seasonal changes in day length and sunlight angle.

Seasons are not mainly caused by changing Sun distance. A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon lies between Sun and Earth and its shadow reaches Earth; a lunar eclipse occurs when Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon. Orbital tilt means eclipses do not happen every month.
lessons.worked: When the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun it has longer days and more direct sunlight; the Southern Hemisphere has the opposite season. A solar eclipse requires a particular alignment at new moon.
lessons.question: Explain why the hemispheres have opposite seasons.
scheme: Earth’s axis is tilted
One hemisphere tilts towards the Sun while the other tilts away
Sunlight angle and day length differ, affecting energy received
lessons.mistake: Earth’s rotation causes day and night; its tilt and orbit cause seasons.

cards.definition: The path of a body moving around another under gravity.
The angle of a body’s rotation axis relative to its orbital orientation.

quiz.q: What mainly causes Earth’s seasons?
opts: A large annual change in Earth–Sun distance.
The Moon blocking sunlight every winter.
Axial tilt changing sunlight angle and day length.
quiz.why: The hemispheres receive different sunlight angles and day lengths as tilted Earth orbits.

misconception.q: In this lesson on orbits, seasons and eclipses, Sam says: “A large annual change in Earth–Sun distance.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Axial tilt changing sunlight angle and day length.
The hemispheres receive different sunlight angles and day lengths as tilted Earth orbits.

lessons.title: Moon phases and space exploration
notes: The Moon reflects sunlight. About half its surface is sunlit at a time, and phases arise because we see different fractions of that illuminated half as it orbits Earth. Ordinary phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow.

New moon has the illuminated side mostly facing away from Earth; full moon has it mostly facing Earth. Exploration uses observations, satellites, probes and sometimes people; evaluate scientific value, cost, risk and limitations rather than assuming every mission has the same purpose.
lessons.worked: A first-quarter Moon appears half illuminated from Earth even though half the whole spherical Moon is sunlit. The name refers to its approximate position through the phase cycle.
lessons.question: Distinguish a normal Moon phase from a lunar eclipse.
scheme: Phases arise from changing views of the sunlit half
Earth’s shadow is not responsible for normal phases
A lunar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes through Earth’s shadow
lessons.mistake: The Moon does not produce its own visible light.

cards.definition: The visible fraction of the Moon’s illuminated half.
The Moon passing through Earth’s shadow.
The Moon’s shadow falling on Earth.

quiz.q: What causes ordinary Moon phases?
opts: The Moon switching its own light on and off.
Our changing view of its sunlit half.
quiz.why: Phases arise from viewing geometry; Earth’s shadow is involved in a lunar eclipse.

misconception.q: In this lesson on moon phases and space exploration, Sam says: “Earth’s shadow every night.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Our changing view of its sunlit half.
Phases arise from viewing geometry; Earth’s shadow is involved in a lunar eclipse.

lessons.title: Friction, drag and deformation
notes: Friction opposes relative sliding or its tendency at a contact. Drag opposes motion through a fluid and generally increases with speed. Forces can change motion or shape, producing stretching, compression or bending.

Use force diagrams and specify the object. Streamlining can reduce drag for suitable conditions. An elastic deformation is reversed when forces are removed; a plastic deformation is permanent. The details depend on material and load.
lessons.worked: A bicycle needs a driving force to balance drag and rolling resistance at a steady speed. With no driving force those resistive forces give a backward resultant and reduce forward speed.
lessons.question: Explain why a cyclist needs a driving force while moving at constant speed on a level road.
scheme: Drag and friction act backwards
Driving force balances them
Zero resultant maintains constant velocity
lessons.mistake: Constant speed needs balanced forces, not necessarily no forces.

cards.definition: A force opposing relative sliding or its tendency at a contact.
A force opposing motion through a fluid.
A permanent change of shape.

quiz.q: Why does a cyclist need a driving force at steady speed?
opts: To create a forward resultant continually.
Because balanced forces mean no movement.
quiz.why: At steady velocity, driving and resistive forces balance rather than vanish.

misconception.q: In this lesson on friction, drag and deformation, Sam says: “To create a forward resultant continually.” Explain the mistake.
ms: To balance friction and drag.
At steady velocity, driving and resistive forces balance rather than vanish.

lessons.title: Stretching springs and Hooke’s law
notes: Extension is the increase in length. For a spring below its limit of proportionality, force is proportional to extension: F=kx. The spring constant k measures stiffness. Extension in metres gives k in N/m.

Measure original length, then add known loads and record settled lengths. Subtract original length and plot force against extension. Repeat, check for permanent stretching and use a safe load limit. Proportionality need not continue indefinitely.
lessons.worked: A spring extends 0.04 m under 6 N, giving k=6/0.04=150 N/m. If it stays in the proportional region, 3 N gives 0.02 m extension.
lessons.question: A spring with k=200 N/m extends by 0.03 m. Calculate force and state a condition for using Hooke’s law.
scheme: F=kx
Spring must be within its proportional region
lessons.mistake: Use extension, not total length, and convert centimetres to metres when needed.

cards.definition: Force divided by extension in a proportional spring region.
The point beyond which force is no longer proportional to extension.

quiz.q: What length belongs in F=kx?
opts: Any measured length of the apparatus.
quiz.why: Extension is stretched length minus original length, in units consistent with k.

misconception.q: In this lesson on stretching springs and hooke’s law, Sam says: “The original spring length.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Extension, not total spring length.
Extension is stretched length minus original length, in units consistent with k.

lessons.title: Levers, turning effects and moments
notes: A moment is a force’s turning effect around a pivot. Moment=force×perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action, measured in N m. A lever can increase a turning effect by increasing this distance.

For rotational equilibrium total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment. Use perpendicular distances, not an arbitrary length to the force application point. Balance of moments alone does not guarantee zero resultant force.
lessons.worked: A 20 N force at 0.3 m gives moment 6 N m. To balance it with an opposite force at 0.6 m requires 10 N, because 10×0.6=6.
lessons.question: A 12 N force acts 0.5 m from a pivot. What opposing force at 0.3 m balances the moment?
scheme: Moment 12×0.5=6 N m
Opposing force satisfies F×0.3=6
F=20 N
lessons.mistake: The distance is perpendicular to the force’s line of action.

cards.definition: The turning effect of a force about a pivot.
The point or axis about which turning occurs.

quiz.q: Which distance is used to calculate a moment?
opts: Perpendicular distance to the force’s line of action.
Any diagonal distance to the load.
The total length of the object.
quiz.why: The effective lever arm is perpendicular to the line of action.

misconception.q: In this lesson on levers, turning effects and moments, Sam says: “Any diagonal distance to the load.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Perpendicular distance to the force’s line of action.
The effective lever arm is perpendicular to the line of action.

lessons.title: Pressure, force and area
notes: Pressure is force per unit area: p=F/A. One pascal is one newton per square metre. For the same perpendicular force, spreading it over a larger area reduces pressure.
Use consistent area units. Convert square units carefully: 1 cm²=0.0001 m². Rearrange F=pA or A=F/p. A pressure increase can result from greater force, smaller area or both.
lessons.worked: A 600 N person supported over 0.03 m² exerts 20,000 Pa. Snowshoes increase contact area, reducing pressure and helping avoid sinking into snow.
lessons.question: A 120 N force acts over 0.04 m². Calculate pressure and explain what doubling the area would do at the same force.
scheme: Pressure is inversely proportional to area for fixed force
Doubling area halves pressure to 1500 Pa
lessons.mistake: Do not treat an area conversion as a length conversion.

cards.definition: Perpendicular force per unit area.
One newton per square metre.

quiz.q: At the same force, what does doubling contact area do?
quiz.why: Pressure = force ÷ area, so it falls when the same force is spread over more area.

misconception.q: In this lesson on pressure, force and area, Sam says: “Doubles pressure.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Halves pressure.
Pressure = force ÷ area, so it falls when the same force is spread over more area.

lessons.title: Gas pressure and particle motion
notes: Gas pressure results from collisions of moving particles with container walls. Each collision exerts a force; pressure is force per unit area. Increasing temperature increases average particle kinetic energy.

For a fixed gas amount and container volume, heating generally increases pressure because collisions are more frequent and more forceful. Compressing a gas at the same temperature increases collision frequency per unit area.
lessons.worked: A sealed rigid container heats up while its gas particle number and volume stay constant. Faster-moving particles transfer more momentum at the walls, so pressure increases.
lessons.question: Explain why squeezing a sealed syringe of air increases its pressure.
scheme: Gas volume falls with particle number unchanged
Particles hit the walls more frequently per unit area
Pressure increases
lessons.mistake: A gas does not need gravity to exert pressure.

cards.definition: Force per unit area caused by particle collisions with surfaces.
A reduction in volume.

quiz.q: Heating a sealed rigid gas container usually does what?
quiz.why: Faster particles make more frequent and more forceful collisions with the fixed walls.

misconception.q: In this lesson on gas pressure and particle motion, Sam says: “Decreases particle number.” Explain the mistake.
ms: Increases pressure.
Faster particles make more frequent and more forceful collisions with the fixed walls.

lessons.title: Liquid pressure, hydraulics and gas investigations
notes: A stationary liquid exerts pressure in all directions, increasing with depth because of the weight of liquid above. In a connected enclosed fluid, an applied pressure change can transmit through the fluid, forming the basis of hydraulics.

Different piston areas give different forces at the same pressure: F=pA. A larger output force trades against smaller output movement in an ideal hydraulic system. Gas experiments must also distinguish changes in temperature, volume and particle amount.
lessons.worked: If pressure is 2000 Pa, a 0.01 m² piston feels 20 N and a 0.05 m² piston 100 N. This does not create energy: the larger piston moves a shorter distance for the same transferred fluid volume.
lessons.question: Explain why a hole lower down a water-filled container can produce a stronger jet.
scheme: Greater depth has more liquid above
Liquid pressure increases with depth
The larger pressure difference drives a faster outflow
lessons.mistake: Pressure and force are different; the same pressure can act over different areas.

cards.definition: A system transmitting a pressure change through an enclosed fluid.
Force per unit area exerted by a liquid.

quiz.q: Why can a hydraulic output piston provide a larger force?
opts: The larger piston always moves farther too.
The same pressure acts over a larger area.
quiz.why: F=pA; in the ideal system a larger force trades against a smaller movement distance.

misconception.q: In this lesson on liquid pressure, hydraulics and gas investigations, Sam says: “The fluid creates extra energy.” Explain the mistake.
ms: The same pressure acts over a larger area.
F=pA; in the ideal system a larger force trades against a smaller movement distance.
